Without it, nothing changes — including the carry-over above. A conversation is scoped to the element and to nobody in particular, and on a shared workstation it will be there for whoever signs in next in the same tab.

For a deployment that keeps history server-side, data-threads-cache="false" stops the local mirror of the message bodies as well, so choosing data-threads-url actually keeps transcripts off the client:

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-threads-url="/agent/threads/" data-threads-cache="false">
</ag-ui-chat>

The client-only concerns (the active thread id, the navigation checkpoint) keep their local store either way, so reloads and navigating tools still work. What is lost is the offline fallback: when the thread endpoint is unreachable the transcript comes back empty rather than stale, and the drawer's offline list loses its previews — a preview being an excerpt of a message, which is the thing being kept off the client. Constructing the store yourself takes the same option:

chat.conversationStore = new RemoteConversationStore(
  "/agent/threads/",
  () => ({ "X-CSRFToken": token }),
  new SessionStorageStore(),
  () => "same-origin",
  false, // cacheMessages
);

RemoteConversationStore.local (read-only) is the store it keeps the client-only state in (the thread pointer and the navigation checkpoint): the third constructor argument, a SessionStorageStore by default. A host wrapping the chat's store reads it to reach what the remote delegates.

A conversation store you assign yourself is never replaced by a change of user-key, whether you assign it before the element connects or after. The one exception is a plain SessionStorageStore assigned before the element connects: that is the same kind as the element's own default, which is all connecting can see, so the element namespaces it as its own and moves it on every key change. Assign it after connecting, or wrap it, to keep it yours. A store that keeps its data somewhere the element cannot see has to scope itself; the element purges only its own sessionStorage namespace and clears what is on screen. If your store wraps a SessionStorageStore, build a new one per principal.

SessionStorageStore.purge(namespace) is the same primitive the element uses, for a host driving its own store from its own sign-out path.

docs.title: Mounting more than one chat on a page
docs.text:
Give each <ag-ui-chat> its own id. The storage namespace is the element's id, falling back to its endpoint — so two elements with no id against the same agent mount (a docked support panel and an inline page assistant, say) would resolve to the same namespace and share a thread pointer, a history drawer and every message key.

They no longer do: the first element to mount keeps the namespace, and a second is given a throwaway one of its own plus a console warning. That keeps the two conversations apart, but the throwaway namespace is minted per mount, so the second element will not restore its conversation across a reload until it has an id.

docs.title: Resuming a run
docs.text:
When the server persists run checkpoints (django-ag-ui's step_store), a run that stopped part-way can be continued rather than restarted. Point the component at the run index and a checkpoints button (an arrow turning back) appears in the header:

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-runs-url="/agent/runs/"></ag-ui-chat>

The panel lists runs the server marked continuable — those with a saved snapshot to seed from. A run that never reached a provider-valid boundary has none, so it isn't offered: resuming it would start from nothing.

A row leads with the run's first user message, from the index's preview field, and shows when it started beside it. That is what makes the list a list of conversations: a time is not an identity, since two runs a minute apart both read "just now", and a run id is not something a person recognises. Where the server sends no preview — an older index, or a run that opened on an image with no caption — the row falls back to the time plus the first eight characters of the id (full id on hover, for correlating with server logs), and so does a row whose preview another row repeats: words shared with a second row identify neither, and one board tends to be asked about more than once. Either way a run that branched from another is marked, so a fork doesn't read as a duplicate of its parent.

Type the next turn in the composer, then pick a row:

  • Resume — continue that run.
  • Fork — branch it, leaving the original untouched.

Both send to the matching server endpoint and stream into the same transcript. The turn you typed is drawn there ahead of the answer and announced with ag-ui-submit, exactly as a send is, so a host that keeps its own record of what the user said sees continued turns too.

Picking a row with an empty composer says so above the input and puts the caret there, rather than closing the panel over nothing: a continuation sends only the new turn, so with nothing typed there is nothing to send.

Picking a row while an answer is still streaming — the conversation's own, or another continuation's — is refused the same way: the hint asks you to wait or stop it, and what you typed stays in the composer for the pick after. The run in flight is not cancelled for you, since a continuation starting over it would leave two answers streaming into one transcript with Stop reaching only one.

Picking a row while a stored conversation is still loading is refused the same way, with a hint asking you to wait for the load: a continuation sends only the new turn, so it must not start before the history it continues is on screen. The wording is the continueWhileLoading string.

docs.title: One URL, three endpoints
docs.text: data-runs-url is the only thing to configure. resume/<id>/ and fork/<id>/ are siblings of the index — django-ag-ui mounts all three under one prefix whenever a step store is set — so they're derived, and there's no way to end up with a half-configured set.

docs.title: The client contract, handled for you
docs.text:
Those endpoints expect a request carrying a fresh run id and only the new turn: the server supplies the prior turns from the snapshot, so re-sending them would duplicate the conversation.

The component satisfies that structurally rather than by remembering a rule. A continuation runs on its own short-lived agent, built pointing at the resume endpoint and seeded with no history — so "only the new turn" is the only thing it can send, and the fresh run id comes free because a new agent mints one. Nothing of the conversation's history goes out on its request.

A resumed run is a normal run in every other respect: frontend tools execute, approval interrupts render their card, headers are re-read per request so a rotated CSRF token or JWT still reaches the endpoint, it carries and updates shared state like any other run, it is bounded by data-max-tool-rounds, and Stop ends it. Its client is built by the same construction as the conversation's own, differing only in the endpoint and the empty seed.

The continued exchange joins the conversation. Its agent holds only the new turn and the answer, and a store keeps one message list per thread, so each save writes the conversation as it stood when you picked the row with the exchange after it — through the same saveMessages as any other run, and as far as it got if it was stopped. A reload then replays the exchange, and the next message you send, now to endpoint again, carries it together with the shared state the continuation left. What is saved is what the transcript shows: a fork's exchange follows the conversation it was picked from, in that same thread.

If the index can't be reached, the panel shows its empty state rather than an error — a history affordance that fails is empty, not broken.

docs.title: The editors on a page of their own
docs.text:
<ag-ui-routines> and <ag-ui-skills> draw the same views the chat opens in its panel, as elements of their own: an inline block that fills its container, for a settings page, a rail or a dialog. Each works alone with only its URL, beside a chat, or under an <ag-ui-agents> provider.

<ag-ui-chat id="chat" endpoint="/agent/" data-routines-url="/agent/routines/"
  data-skill-editor-url="/agent/skills/editor/" data-editors="external"></ag-ui-chat>
<section class="settings">
  <ag-ui-routines for="chat"></ag-ui-routines>
  <ag-ui-skills for="chat"></ag-ui-skills>
</section>

<script type="module">
  import { defineChat } from "@artooi/agents-web-components/chat";
  import { defineRoutines } from "@artooi/agents-web-components/routines";
  import { defineSkills } from "@artooi/agents-web-components/skills";
  defineChat();
  defineRoutines();
  defineSkills();
</script>

Both elements share these rules:

  • Binding. for names a chat's id, looked up in the element's own root; a chat added later is picked up when it first reports its thread. Or set the chat property, which wins over for until it is set back to null. With neither, the element binds to the chat of an <ag-ui-agents> provider: the one its agents attribute names by id, else the nearest one around it, and loads again when the agent it moves to lists a different URL. A chat or provider whose element is not defined yet is waited for, then bound. Until it binds, an element with its own URL loads it alone, through fetch, and loads it again through the chat or provider once bound. provider (read-only) is that provider. Bound to nothing, the element works alone.
  • URL. Its own URL attribute wins; else the bound chat's same attribute; else, under a provider, the URL the agent on screen lists in the directory. With none, the element draws nothing. url (read-only) is the one in use, and reload() reads it again from the list.
  • Requests. Bound to a chat, they go through chat.request(); under a provider, through provider.request(), which sends the provider's headers and getHeaders(); so the headers and cookie policy are the ones the page already set. Alone, they go through fetch with the credentials attribute (omit, same-origin by default, or include). Either way the element's own data-csrf-token, or else the cookie data-csrf-cookie names, read at each request, is sent as data-csrf-header (X-CSRFToken by default), winning per header. request(url, init?) is that fetch.
  • Opening from the chat. With data-editors="external" on the chat, its Skills and Routines buttons, Make this a routine and the palette's Manage skills fire ag-ui-open-editor (OPEN_EDITOR_EVENT, detail { editor, fromConversation }, where editor is routines or skills; bubbling, composed and cancelable) instead of opening the panel. A bound element answers it: it calls preventDefault(), takes focus on its heading and, for Make this a routine, opens the new routine's form. Scroll it into view or open the dialog it sits in from your own listener. Without an element to answer, nothing opens.
  • Focus. The list has no back arrow; a form's arrow steps back to the list. A redraw moves focus only when focus was already inside the element.
  • Styling. The full-panel view's parts (panel-view, panel-view-bar, panel-view-title, panel-view-body, panel-view-footer, back-button) and the view's own, as listed under Theming. The chat's colour, font and size tokens apply, plus --ag-ui-danger. The element takes the page's color-scheme, unless its theme attribute names light, dark or auto.
  • Strings. strings translates the view's text, merged over the English, with the same keys as the chat's strings for that view, plus back (the arrow's label).

Neither element is in the main /bundle. Without a build step, load /routines/bundle or /skills/bundle; each carries the element and its view, and none of the chat or the provider.

docs.title: The routines element
docs.text:
<ag-ui-routines> reads data-routines-url (django-ag-ui's routines/, from 0.86.0). The list, Pause or Resume, Run now and the form are the chat's routines view.

  • Make this a routine is at the foot of the list while the bound chat has a prompt on screen, and follows that conversation as it moves on. makeRoutine() opens the form the same way. Bound to nothing, it is absent.
  • The form's time and timezone take a child of the element with slot="routine-time" or slot="routine-timezone", and its data-routine-minute-step, as on the chat: see The time and timezone fields.
  • A last result fires ag-ui-routines-open-thread (ROUTINES_OPEN_THREAD_EVENT, detail { threadId }, bubbling, composed and cancelable). Unless a listener prevents it, a chat bound by for or the property switches to that thread, and a provider opens it on the agent on screen. Alone, the event is all there is.
  • Strings are AgUiRoutinesStrings, the chat's routines keys (routines, newRoutine, makeRoutine, pause, resume, runNow and the form's) plus back, "Back to the routines" by default.

docs.title: The skills element
docs.text:
<ag-ui-skills> reads data-skill-editor-url (django-ag-ui's skills/editor/, from 0.83.0). The list, Turn on and the form are the chat's skill editor.

  • Draft one with the agent sends /create-skill to the bound chat. Bound to nothing, it is absent.
  • The palette follows. After each write, the element calls the bound chat's refreshSkills(). When a run in that chat sends django-ag-ui's ag_ui.skills_changed CUSTOM event, the list reloads.
  • Strings are AgUiSkillsStrings, the chat's skill editor keys (skills, newSkill, noSkills, draftSkill, writeSkill, turnOn, turnOff and the form's) plus back, "Back to the skills" by default.

docs.title: New chat and collapse
docs.text:
The header carries built-in buttons for a new chat (a pencil on a square), maximize (two arrows pointing out) and collapse (a chevron down, or on a sidebar a panel closing into its edge; data-collapse-icon chooses it). The matching JS API:

  • newChat() — clears the transcript, drops the in-memory run state, and mints a new thread id. The conversation it leaves is kept: it stays in the history drawer to return to, and on a server-backed store it stays on the server. Deleting one is the drawer row's own action. A chat nothing was ever sent in is the exception — it was never listed, so it is dropped rather than left behind. Focus moves to the composer, whichever control started the new chat, unless the widget is collapsed, and the page is not scrolled to it. A restore still loading or replaying the conversation being left stops there, so nothing of it is drawn into the new chat, and a run it was about to resume after a reload is not resumed: coming back to that conversation later answers the interrupted call as not finished. Called before the element connects (or while it is out of the document), it waits: threadId stays null and nothing fires until the element connects, which then starts the new chat, so the one ag-ui-thread event is a new.
  • describeSurface() — where the panel is and what can be done to it: placement, collapsed, maximized (read-only), what it collapses to (collapseTo), whether it can be moved, whether it fills the screen, its box and the viewport. movable folds the two reasons a move can fail into the one answer a caller needs.
  • moveTo(corner) — send the panel to top-left / top-right / bottom-left / bottom-right, returning whether it went. It takes the axes the same way a user drag does, so the launcher travels with it and switching placement hands them back. Returns false rather than pretending when the placement owns its position or the panel fills the screen. Under collapse-to="bar" or "none" it moves the panel within the room above the bar or the anchor.
  • resetSize() — drop the size the user dragged in the current placement, and its stored copy, so the placement's own size and your --ag-ui-width / --ag-ui-height apply again; sizes dragged in other placements are kept. For a host that enters a sized state of its own (an expanded mode) instead of the built-in maximize: a user's drag outranks host tokens, so call this first. Under collapse-to="bar" or "none" it also returns a panel the user dragged off its dock to the dock and forgets the stored spot; a corner panel under auto keeps its dragged position.
  • setCollapsed(collapsed) / toggleCollapsed() — collapse or expand the widget. The state is reflected as the boolean collapsed attribute/property and persisted per-tab in sessionStorage, so it survives a reload.

Each change emits an ag-ui-toggle event (the TOGGLE_EVENT constant) with detail: { collapsed: boolean } (typed ToggleDetail), so a host can mirror the state in its own chrome — or hide the built-in toggle and drive the collapsed attribute itself.

chat.newChat();
chat.toggleCollapsed();
chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-toggle", (e) => console.log(e.detail.collapsed));

docs.title: The header row and its More menu
docs.text:
The header shows every control it has while they fit. When they stop fitting, or when the row would hold more than five, the optional controls move into a More menu (the three dots), one at a time in this order: the theme toggle, Skills, checkpoints, then History. New chat, Maximize and Collapse always stay in the row. Once anything has moved, the row holds at most four controls beside More, so a header with every opt-in on still fits a 240px panel with its title readable. With data-routines-url set, More also holds Make this a routine (the last item, in the menu only) while the conversation on screen has a prompt, and it counts toward that cap, so the first prompt may move a control into the menu.

Nothing to opt into, and nothing a host drives changes: a control in the menu is the same <button>, with the same class (header-btn--history), part and icon-* slot, so ::part(history-button) still styles it and shadowRoot.querySelector(".header-btn--history").click() still opens the drawer. In the menu it is a menuitem row showing its glyph and its name. The menu takes ::part(header-menu) and the button ::part(more-button); its name is the moreControls string. From the keyboard, Enter, Space or the down arrow on More opens the menu on its first row (the up arrow on its last); the arrows, Home and End move between rows, Escape closes it and returns focus to More, and Tab or a click elsewhere closes it.

docs.title: Maximizing the panel
docs.text:
The maximize control (two arrows pointing out, maximize-button part, icon-maximize slot) grows the open panel, and pressed again it restores it (the arrows point in). It is labelled "Maximize" and "Restore" (the maximize and restore strings), apart from the launcher's and the rail's "Expand", which opens the panel.

  • Where it is offered. A corner panel (floating, bottom-left, the default) and a docked one (collapse-to="bar" or "none") grow on both axes; sidebar and side grow in width only. page, full and embedded have no control, and neither does any viewport of 600px or less, data-small-viewport="off" included. The control is absent from the header there, not hidden, and the state is refused: a panel maximized when its placement switches to one of these, or when the window narrows to 600px, leaves it.
  • What it grows to. --ag-ui-maximized-width and --ag-ui-maximized-height, which default to the panel's cap (--ag-ui-max-width / --ag-ui-max-height, the room the host left less one gutter). A side column reads the width only.
  • The drag. Entering it takes the dragged size off without forgetting it, and the resize grips are hidden while it lasts. Restoring, and collapsing (which leaves the state), put the placement's own size back, or the size the user dragged in it.
  • The API. chat.maximized (reflected as the maximized attribute), setMaximized(bool) and toggleMaximized(). Each change emits ag-ui-maximize (the MAXIMIZE_EVENT constant) with detail: { maximized } (typed MaximizeDetail). It fires only while connected: a markup maximized is announced once at connect, and only if it holds (a panel that mounts collapsed announces nothing), and a change made while detached is announced once on reconnect, only if it differs from what listeners last heard. It is not stored: a reload opens at the placement's own size. describeSurface() reports it, and no agent tool changes it.
chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-maximize", (e) => console.log(e.detail.maximized));

ag-ui-chat { --ag-ui-maximized-width: 960px; --ag-ui-maximized-height: 85vh; }

--ag-ui-min-page-width keeps that much of the page beside a sidebar or side column: it caps the column's width at the viewport less it, whether the width was dragged, set by --ag-ui-width, or maximized. It is unset by default, which caps nothing.

ag-ui-chat[placement="sidebar"] { --ag-ui-min-page-width: 480px; }

A host that wants its own sized state can still build it: hide the control (ag-ui-chat::part(maximize-button) { display: none }), slot a button into header-actions, set its own --ag-ui-width / --ag-ui-height in a class, and call resetSize() as it enters, so a dragged size does not outrank its tokens.

docs.title: Driving the conversation from your own chrome
docs.text:
A host that lists conversations in its own bar, rather than in the built-in drawer, drives the one on screen with the drawer's own paths:

  • switchThread(threadId) — put a stored thread on screen and replay it, as picking its row in the drawer does. Returns a Promise<void> that resolves once the thread is drawn. A run in flight is cancelled, as the drawer and newChat() cancel it; read running first if you would rather wait. Switching to the thread already on screen does nothing, and so does a call before the element connects; a second call for the thread that is still loading settles with that load, after the replay. If the store rejects the load, the element stays on the thread it was on, redraws it, fires no ag-ui-thread, and the promise rejects with the store's error.
  • deleteThread(threadId) — delete a stored thread, as the drawer row's delete does. Deleting the thread on screen cancels its run and puts a fresh thread in its place; deleting another leaves the screen alone. Prefer it to conversationStore.clear(), which deletes the record and nothing else: the run, the transcript and the drawer are left pointing at it.
  • threadId (read-only) — the thread on screen, null before the element first connects. It only reads. conversationStore.threadId() mints and stores a thread when the store points at none, so asking it which conversation is showing can start one.
  • threadTitle (read-only) — the title of the thread on screen, "" while nothing has been sent in it. A title renamed here, or one the conversation list shows that the messages do not derive (a server's own), wins; otherwise it is the first user message, and a first message that is exactly a skill's /token reads as that skill's catalog title, else as the token in words (/summarize_draw reads "Summarize draw"). It is set on the first send, before the server lists the thread. Every change fires one ag-ui-thread-title event (THREAD_TITLE_EVENT, detail { threadId, title }, typed ThreadTitleDetail), after the ag-ui-thread event of the change that caused it. title-text="auto" draws it without a listener.
  • running (read-only) — whether an interaction is in flight: the composer's own state, the one it shows Stop for, across every tool round, a Retry and a checkpoint continuation as well as a send. Reflected on the element as the data-running attribute, written by the element rather than by you, as data-empty is, so the chrome around the chat can style on it.

Every change of conversation fires one ag-ui-thread event (the THREAD_EVENT constant), after the transcript has been replaced, so a listener reads the conversation it is told about. detail is { threadId, previousThreadId, reason } (typed ThreadDetail). previousThreadId is the thread the previous event reported, null before the first, and reason is one of:

reason When new newChat() or the built-in New chat button. switch switchThread() or a row picked in the drawer. Two switches made before the first had replayed report only the second. delete The thread on screen was deleted, and a fresh one took its place. restore The stored thread was replayed: when the element connects (previousThreadId is null the first time), or by reload(). rescope A user-key change handed the element to another principal, live or while it was out of the document.

A page reload keeps restoring the thread, as MPA durability describes, and reports it as restore. Ignore a reason you do not know: more may be added.

chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-thread", (e) => myBar.markActive(e.detail.threadId));
myBar.onPick = (threadId) => chat.switchThread(threadId);

docs.title: Open threads (tabs)
docs.text:
A host that draws conversations as tabs keeps the open set on the element rather than beside it. The element draws nothing for it: the tabs are the host's chrome. Tracking starts at the host's first openTab, which opens the thread on screen with it, or at connect when this tab already stored a set. Until then nothing is kept, written or announced, so a host that never calls openTab sees no change.

  • tabs (read-only) — the open threads in the order they were opened, each { threadId, title } (typed ThreadTab), frozen. title is "" until one is known. Empty until tracking starts.
  • openTab(threadId, title?) — open a thread as the last tab without showing it; switchThread shows it. Without a title, the store's list names it. A thread already open stays where it is.
  • closeTab(threadId) — close a tab. The thread stays in history, which is what sets a close apart from deleteThread. Closing the thread on screen shows the next tab, else the one before it, else a new chat, cancelling a run in flight as switchThread does.

Once tracking has started, showing a thread opens it: switchThread, newChat, the drawer, a child-session link and the parent breadcrumb each open the thread they show (a link or breadcrumb a host prevents shows nothing and adds no tab), so the thread on screen always has a tab, except when a closed tab's neighbour cannot be loaded. A new chat leaving a thread nothing was sent in takes over that thread's tab, since the store drops the empty thread. deleteThread closes the tab as it deletes the thread.

The set is kept per browser tab in sessionStorage, under the conversation's namespace (the element's id and user-key, or, under <ag-ui-agents>, the agent's: agent:<id>, so each agent keeps its own tabs), so a reload reads the same tabs back, titles included. A user-key handover drops the previous user's tabs; a first user-key naming the user already there keeps them.

Every change fires one ag-ui-tabs event (TABS_EVENT, detail { tabs, reason }, typed TabsDetail), with reason one of open, close, delete, title, restore (connect or reload()) and rescope (a user-key handover). Ignore a reason you do not know. A thread shown is in tabs by the time its ag-ui-thread fires, and its ag-ui-tabs follows. Switching between two open tabs changes no tab, so mark the active one from ag-ui-thread.

chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-tabs", (e) => myTabs.draw(e.detail.tabs));
chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-thread", (e) => myTabs.markActive(e.detail.threadId));
chat.openTab(chat.threadId); // start tracking
myTabs.onPick = (threadId) => chat.switchThread(threadId);
myTabs.onClose = (threadId) => chat.closeTab(threadId);

docs.title: The composer's own keys
docs.text:
Enter during a run queues. A second run cannot start while one is in flight — it would orphan the first — so that key used to do nothing at all, silently. A checkpoint continuation picked from the panel counts as in flight from the pick rather than from its first event, which is a request later, so a turn typed in that gap is parked too rather than racing it. What is waiting shows above the composer as chips, each of which takes its message back when pressed, and the next one is sent when the run settles. Stopping the run discards them: sending into a conversation someone has just stopped is the opposite of what stopping meant. Nothing is lost, though — a queued message entered the recall history below when it left the composer, so Up gets it back after a Stop, and after its chip is taken back.

The composer also walks back through what you have already sent, on Up and Down — the shape every shell and every coding agent uses. It holds every turn that left the composer: one sent at once, one queued behind a run (from the moment it is queued), and one sent to resume or fork a run from the checkpoint panel. A message sent with sendMessage is not in it, because it was never typed there. Only from an empty composer and only with the skills palette closed: an arrow inside text is how you move the caret, and taking it unconditionally would break editing to add a shortcut. Arrowing forward past the newest turn empties the box again, so the way out is the key that got you in. A walk lasts only while the composer holds the turn it put there: anything else that writes the box — typing, a quotation, a skill, dictation, or the host page itself — ends it, so the next arrow moves the caret in what was written rather than replacing it. The history is this conversation's: starting a new chat, switching threads or changing user-key clears it with the transcript.

docs.title: Collapsing to the launcher
docs.text:
A collapsed widget shrinks to a floating launcher in the corner it already occupies: the panel scales down into it and fades, the launcher grows out of the same point, and clicking the launcher reverses it. Only transform and opacity animate, so the motion is compositor-only and never reflows your page. Two placements collapse to something else instead — sidebar slides out to its edge rail, and embedded / page keep the header bar, since one is laid out by your page and the other is a full-screen route.

The launcher's mark comes from the same seam as the header icon, most specific first: a slotted slot="launcher" child, then data-launcher-icon-url, then data-icon-url, then the built-in speech bubble.

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-launcher-icon-url="/mark.svg"></ag-ui-chat>

<!-- or any markup at all -->
<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/">
  <svg slot="launcher" width="26" height="26"><!-- ... --></svg>
</ag-ui-chat>

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-launcher-size: 48px;
  --ag-ui-launcher-radius: 14px;  /* 50% for a circle */
  --ag-ui-launcher-bg: #14532d;   /* defaults to the panel background */
  --ag-ui-launcher-fg: #ffffff;   /* defaults to the text colour */
  --ag-ui-launcher-icon-size: 22px;
  --ag-ui-launcher-inset: auto 0 0 auto;  /* which corner of the widget's box */
}

The sizes and defaults above are Quiet's. The other themes bring their own launcher: classic the 56px circle in the header's colours, soft a 56px accent tile, and ledger a 44px tile in the text colour.

The collapsed host keeps its box. Animating the element's own width and height would animate layout; instead the box stays put with pointer-events: none, and the launcher takes the clicks. A host measuring getBoundingClientRect() on a collapsed widget still sees the panel's footprint — nothing there paints or takes input.

docs.title: The unread badge
docs.text:
A collapsed widget is the one state where an answer can arrive with nothing on screen to say so, so the launcher carries a count of the answers that finished while it was closed (capped at 9+). It is the only affordance here that is on by default; data-unread-badge="false" turns the badge off.

Unseen answers are kept per thread. Each answer counts against the thread it ran on, and a thread is read only when it is on screen and the panel is expanded. On screen in a collapsed panel is not read. So an answer that finished on thread A while collapsed stays unread across a collapsed switch to B, a newChat(), or an expand on B, and is read once A is on screen in the open panel. unread is the total across threads, which is what the badge shows; it shows on the collapsed launcher only, so an open panel whose other threads hold unseen answers shows no badge. A principal change (a new user-key) drops the previous principal's marks, and deleting a thread drops its own.

A store can carry read state across pages and devices, through two optional members. The element fetches the thread list when the drawer opens or a thread switches, not at page load, so a store's unread rows are counted from that fetch on: a page that never opens the drawer shows no badge for answers that finished elsewhere.

  • ThreadMeta.unread (boolean): a thread listThreads() reports as unread, and the page has not counted, counts once, when the list is fetched.
  • markRead(threadId): called when the element reads a thread with unseen answers, and when the run of an answer that finished on the thread in view settles (after the answer, so a server has saved it first). A server store maps it to its read endpoint, and should list the thread with unread: false afterwards.

A store without either still has its threads counted and cleared in the page. Neither is implemented by the default SessionStorageStore.

The count is also the launcher's accessible name (Expand — 2 unread, from the expandUnread string), because a coloured dot says nothing to a screen reader.

docs.title: Moving the launcher
docs.text:
The collapsed launcher can be dragged anywhere on screen, and it stays there — per tab, in sessionStorage, namespaced per element exactly like the collapsed, theme and size preferences. Arrow keys move it from the keyboard (Shift for a larger step). data-launcher-drag="false" turns it off; so does any placement that already places the launcher itself — sidebar collapses it to a full-height rail, embedded and page hide it and keep their header bar, and a full-bleed panel has no clear space to open into.

The panel then opens into whichever side of the launcher has more room. For each axis the element compares the space a panel would have on either side of the launcher and pins the side with more of it, so a launcher dragged to the top-left opens down and to the right. What it compares is the room the panel would get, not which half of the screen the launcher is in — those give different answers either side of centre, and only the first one is about whether the panel fits.

A launcher parked where the panel fits neither way — the middle of a short viewport — keeps its position anyway: the panel is clamped into the viewport and the launcher carries the difference, which is why it can end up sitting outside its own host box. Nothing clips it there.

A drag writes --ag-ui-inset and --ag-ui-launcher-inset on the host, and an inline custom property outranks your stylesheet's rule for the same one — the same trade a dragged size makes against a placement. Switching to a placement that places itself hands both back.

An undragged launcher is untouched. With nothing stored, the element writes neither property and your CSS decides, exactly as before. The geometry is built so that feeding it the resting position reproduces the default auto 24px 24px auto unchanged.

docs.title: Moving the panel
docs.text:
An open panel moves by its header, the way a window moves by its title bar.

The launcher travels the same distance. Drag the panel 100px left and the bubble it collapses into is 100px left of where it was — it is one widget being moved, not two things being placed. The distance is the panel's own, so a panel held against the viewport's margin stops and the bubble stops with it, and the bubble is then held on screen in its own right.

A position you state is kept, not re-derived. That is the difference between the two drags: a launcher drag says where the bubble goes and lets the panel open into whatever room the viewport has, which is re-decided on every expand and every window resize; a header drag states the panel's own position, so it survives collapsing, reopening and reloading. Dragging the bubble again hands the decision back. Both are stored per tab, and data-launcher-drag="false" turns off both.

Which corner the panel is pinned by is re-picked when the drag ends, from where the bubble has ended up, so the next expand still opens into clear space. Re-picking it moves nothing: the corner only says which edges the two insets are written from, and both are written from positions that are already decided.

The controls in the header keep their own presses — a drag started on a button, a link or a field never begins, including one you slot in.

There is no keyboard shortcut on the header, deliberately. A header is not a control, and making it focusable would put a tab stop with no role ahead of the controls a keyboard user came for — while arrow keys on the collapsed launcher already move the widget, panel included.

chat.unread; // 2

// Every change, whether or not the badge renders it — so a host that hides the
// badge can put the count in its own chrome. `threadIds` names the threads the
// change marked or cleared, and is empty for a collapse toggle that touched none.
chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-unread", (e) => setDockBadge(e.detail.unread, e.detail.threadIds));

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-badge-bg: #b91c1c;   /* defaults to --ag-ui-danger */
  --ag-ui-badge-fg: #ffffff;
  --ag-ui-badge-size: 18px;
  --ag-ui-badge-font-size: 11px;
}

docs.title: Collapsing to a bottom bar
docs.text:
collapse-to chooses what a collapsed panel becomes, for a host whose layout has a bottom toolbar. It is opt-in: absent, auto, or any other value leaves every placement as the sections above describe. It is live, like placement.

  • bar: the component's own bar. A strip along the whole bottom edge of the viewport, in place of the round launcher: the title, the unread badge, and a running indicator while an interaction is in flight. Pressing the strip toggles the panel, which rises from the bar's right end with the bar still beneath it as the minimise target. The bar's history button opens the conversation list as a popover above the bar, without expanding the panel, its outer edge in line with the panel's on a wide viewport, and a second press closes it; openThreads() while collapsed opens it too. Expanding the panel closes the popover, so the panel opens on the conversation. It replaces the launcher only, so it applies to the corner placements, side and full: sidebar keeps its rail, embedded its header bar, and page has no collapsed state at all.
  • none: your own bar. Collapsed is hidden: nothing of the widget is left to see or hit, under every collapsible placement. Your bar's button drives the public API (collapsed, toggleCollapsed()), and anchor names the element the panel rises from, right-aligned to it. An anchor that resolves to nothing opens the panel from the placement's own corner, with one console warning. While collapsed, openThreads() opens the conversation list as a popover beside the anchor, or beside the element you pass as openThreads({ anchor }), which wins over the attribute and property for that call. It opens below a button in the top half of the viewport and above one in the bottom half, right-aligned to it and held inside the window (full width less 8px on a phone). Picking a conversation switches to it and closes the list, and leaves the panel collapsed: you get ag-ui-thread and decide whether to expand. Escape, a press outside, closeThreads() and expanding the panel close it; a press on the button itself does not, so your button can toggle the list. With no anchor at all, openThreads() warns once per call and draws nothing. embedded hides the whole element while collapsed under none, so it has no popover.
<nav class="toolbar">
  <!-- ... -->
  <button id="agent-button" type="button">Agent</button>
</nav>
<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" collapse-to="none" anchor="#agent-button"></ag-ui-chat>
<script type="module">
  const chat = document.querySelector("ag-ui-chat");
  const button = document.getElementById("agent-button");
  button.addEventListener("click", () => chat.toggleCollapsed());
  // Under none the element announces the state it mounted in, once, so the
  // button can be labelled before anyone presses it.
  chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-toggle", (e) => {
    button.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(!e.detail.collapsed));
  });
</script>

Clearing your toolbar. Under none the panel stands --ag-ui-anchor-gap (default 8px) above the anchor's top edge. The anchor is the button, not the toolbar around it, so a button sitting inside a taller toolbar puts the panel's foot across the toolbar's top border. Set the gap to the button's distance from the toolbar's top plus the clearance you want:

/* The button stands 7px below the toolbar's top edge; clear it by 8px. */
ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-anchor-gap: 15px;
}

A gap wider than the gutter is taken off the panel's max height as well, so a tall panel still stops at the top of the window.

A button in a header. The panel opens on the side of the anchor with more room, so a button in a top header opens it below the button and one in a bottom bar opens it above, with no inset of your own. anchor-side="above" or "below" fixes the side; auto, the default, decides again when the window is resized (never during a drag), so an anchor near the middle of the window can change sides. Below the anchor the gap is measured from the button's bottom edge, and the max height is the room under it less one gutter. On either side the panel lines up with the anchor's right edge unless that would put either edge inside the 24px gutter of the window, where it stops instead; its width cap is the window less two gutters, maximized included.

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" collapse-to="none" anchor="#agent-button" anchor-side="below"></ag-ui-chat>

Under none the element dispatches ag-ui-toggle once as it connects, with whichever state it mounted in, collapsed or open. Under auto and bar it does not, as before. That event touches neither the stored state nor the unread count.

The page's space is yours. The bar is fixed over the page, so a host pads its own page by the bar's height. The component never writes your CSS, and a custom property cannot carry the height up to your page (it inherits down, never up), so it hands you a number: barHeight (CSS px, read-only) and an ag-ui-bar-height event (the BAR_HEIGHT_EVENT constant, detail { height }) on every change, including a font-size change. Both read 0 where no bar is drawn: under auto and none, on a phone while the panel is open, and while your size fills the window with the panel open. If you write the height into --ag-ui-viewport-inset-bottom, a panel that fills the box that leaves stays judged against that box once the bar goes and the box grows by the bar's height: it settles with the bar gone and room at its foot. Writing some other share of the height does not settle; publish it to your page as below.

const chat = document.querySelector("ag-ui-chat");
const pad = () => {
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--chat-bar-height", `${chat.barHeight}px`);
};
chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-bar-height", pad);
pad();

body {
  padding-bottom: var(--chat-bar-height, 0px);
}

A fixed sidebar pushes your page the same way. A docked placement="sidebar" (or "side") is fixed over the page, so dockWidth (CSS px, read-only) and an ag-ui-dock-width event (the DOCK_WIDTH_EVENT constant, detail { width, side }, side being "left" or "right", as data-side says) hand you the width it covers at rest: the panel's width while open, the rail's (--ag-ui-rail-width, 52 by default) while collapsed to it, and 0 under collapse-to="none" or a launcher, under every other placement, on a phone while the panel is open, and under --ag-ui-position: static, where your own layout already makes room. The event fires once per change of the resting value, never per frame of the width transition, and once at the end of a resize drag.

const chat = document.querySelector("ag-ui-chat");
const push = () => {
  const { dockWidth: width } = chat;
  const side = document.querySelector("ag-ui-chat").getAttribute("data-side") ?? "right";
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--chat-dock-left", side === "left" ? `${width}px` : "0px");
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--chat-dock-right", side === "left" ? "0px" : `${width}px`);
};
chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-dock-width", push);
push();

body {
  padding-left: var(--chat-dock-left, 0px);
  padding-right: var(--chat-dock-right, 0px);
}

No inset needed. Under bar and none you do not set --ag-ui-inset to keep the panel off your toolbar: its max height is the viewport less the bar's height (or, under none, the distance to the anchor's top, or below it from the anchor's bottom) and one gutter, and its bottom sits on the bar or the anchor (its top, when it opens below).

Docked, and still movable. On a wide viewport a docked corner panel (the corner placements under bar, or under none with or without an anchor) moves by its header, and moveTo moves it, as it would the corner panel it is; describeSurface() reports movable: true. There is no launcher to drag: the bar and your own control stay where they are.

  • Above the dock. A dragged panel stays inside the viewport and above the bar's top edge, so it never covers the bar it minimises to. Under none with an anchor it stays above the anchor's top edge the same way (below its bottom edge, when the panel opens below it), because the anchor is your own way back and has to stay in view; --ag-ui-anchor-gap no longer applies once the panel is dragged, and the screen-edge margin (8px) does. Under none with no anchor only the viewport holds it, as for a corner panel.
  • Remembered like a corner panel. Minimising and reopening brings it back where it was dragged, and so does a reload. The spot is kept apart from the one a corner panel stores under auto, so switching collapse-to never puts one surface's spot on the other. A spot that no longer fits, because the window shrank or the bar grew, is held inside the room that is left and comes back whole when there is room again.
  • Resizing. A panel standing on its dock keeps the edges on the bar or the anchor still and the free ones follow the grip. Once dragged off, every edge follows its grip, as on a corner panel.
  • Back to the dock. resetSize() drops the placement's dragged size and returns the panel to its dock, forgetting the stored spot, so a reload opens it there too.
  • Keeping it fixed. data-launcher-drag="false" turns the header drag and moveTo off here as everywhere else, and the panel stays on its dock.
  • A host's size that fills the window. Set --ag-ui-width and --ag-ui-height to the whole window, with --ag-ui-max-width and --ag-ui-max-height out of the way (the defaults stop short of it), and the panel stands at the start of the room you left free, whether it was moved or not. The bar and the grips go while it does, as on a phone, with barHeight at 0 and the header's minimise control as the way back. The bar comes back when the panel is collapsed, and both when your size stops filling. The stored spot stays, and the panel goes back to it, or to its dock, once your size stops filling. An inline --ag-ui-inset of your own stays where you wrote it.

Placements that own their position (side and full under bar, sidebar and embedded under none) do not move, as without collapse-to.

Phones. At 600px or less the open panel stays full-bleed, over the bar, and the header's minimise control is the way back; the bar shows only while collapsed, so no second strip sits at the bottom edge while the keyboard is up. The panel does not move there, and a spot dragged on a wide viewport does not apply: it comes back when the window is wide again.

The bar is styled through the parts bar (the strip's wrapper, holding the launcher, the place and the history button) and bar-history, and the launcher's own parts (launcher, rail-label, launcher-badge) inside it.

The place in the bar. When getPlace (or the route map standing in for it) names a place, the strip shows it beside the title as quiet secondary text: the bar-place part holding place-label and place-detail, the parts the chip uses. It comes from the chip's one read, so refreshPlace(), popstate and a withheld place update it as they update the chip. A long place truncates with an ellipsis before the history button leaves the strip, and no place draws nothing. A place the user withheld stays in the strip dashed and struck through (data-excluded on bar-place), because the bar must not claim the page is sent. The phone strip, shown while collapsed, carries it too.

docs.title: Resizing the panel
docs.text:
The panel carries a grip on every edge and every corner, so it can be dragged from whichever side you are already near.

  • placement="page" gets no grips — a full-bleed layout is 100vw/100vh by definition, so there is nothing to drag.
  • placement="sidebar" keeps only the two vertical edges; the placement owns the height, so a horizontal edge or a corner would advertise a drag that does nothing.
  • Everything else gets all eight.

The edge a grip does not drag is the one that stays put. That is the whole model: the left grip moves the left edge and holds the right, the right grip does the reverse, a corner does both axes. A grip names its own edge, so no layout can invert it.

docs.title: Dragging the edge your layout was holding still
docs.text:
A floating panel pinned bottom-right cannot grow rightward on its own — its right edge is what the placement fixed. So a drag on a pinned edge moves the panel as well as resizing it, and the component takes the position over by writing --ag-ui-inset, the same ownership a dragged launcher takes.

A grip on a free edge writes nothing but the size, exactly as before, so a host positioning the panel with its own rule keeps that rule until someone drags the edge it was holding.

Which edges those are belongs to your CSS rather than to placement — a floating panel a host right-aligns is anchored bottom-left — so the element probes its own geometry and reflects the result as data-resize-anchor (e.g. bottom-right means those two edges are fixed). Nothing in the stylesheet reads it any more; the element uses it to decide what a drag on a pinned edge costs, and which grip carries the keyboard.

The probe shrinks rather than grows. Growing by a pixel cannot answer the question at a size already resting against max-width or max-height: the box does not change, no edge moves, and every clamped axis reads as pinned on the side that is actually free. That was reachable with no user action at all — the default panel is 380px wide against a max-width of 100vw - 48px, so any viewport under 428px was born clamped, with the grip on the wrong corner and the drag inverted.

docs.title: Sizes, keyboard, and parts
docs.text:
A drag writes the private --_drag-width / --_drag-height on the host, not your --ag-ui-width / --ag-ui-height tokens, which stay yours. The precedence is:

  • Above 600px, the dragged size beats a host's --ag-ui-width / --ag-ui-height, !important included, so a user who resized the panel keeps their size. A host that enters a sized state of its own (an "expanded" class) calls resetSize() when it does, which drops the current placement's dragged size and its stored copy and hands control back to the host tokens. A host with no such state needs nothing.
  • Per placement. A dragged size belongs to the placement it was dragged in and is stored under it: absent and floating share one, and bottom-left, sidebar, side and embedded each keep their own (data-side is not a placement, so a left and a right sidebar share one). Switching placement swaps in the new placement's size, or its default when it has none, so a placement switch needs no resetSize(). A collapse-to change keeps the size. A size stored by a release before this one is read as floating's.
  • At 600px or less, the small-viewport shape ignores the dragged size entirely, for the placements that block covers (floating, bottom-left, sidebar, side and the default): the panel is full-bleed whatever was dragged or stored, and a window narrowed after a wide-window drag goes full-bleed too. page is already that shape, and embedded is left to the host's own box, so neither is touched by the block. data-small-viewport="off" keeps a dragged size at every width on the covered placements.

A dragged size is a private property, so a host should not read it back from the element's inline style; use getBoundingClientRect(), or resetSize() to clear it.

A custom property alone does not leave placement in charge — an inline custom property still outranks a :host([placement=…]) rule setting the same property. So the component enforces the split directly: a placement owns the axes it fixes, and a dragged or persisted size is only ever applied to the ones it leaves free. Switching placement hands the owned axes back. Without that, a height dragged while floating capped a docked sidebar that had asked for 100vh.

A host rule that sizes the element wins over both. ag-ui-chat { flex: 1 } stretches the panel to its container and the dragged width has no visible effect — which reads as a broken control rather than as your stylesheet winning. Give the element flex: 0 1 auto (plus max-width: 100%) if it lives in a flex container.

The size persists per tab (sessionStorage, namespaced per element like the collapsed and theme preferences) and is restored before the first paint.

Exactly one grip is in the tab order — the corner diagonally opposite the pinned one, so an arrow key changes the size and never the position. Eight separators between the transcript and the composer would be a keyboard obstacle rather than keyboard parity, and one grip already reaches both axes. Arrow keys resize from it (Shift for a larger step).

Each grip draws a short pill centred on its edge — a dot in a corner — on hover and focus as well as during a drag. The hit area and the mark are separate on purpose: the area is the whole strip, so the grip is easy to catch, while the mark stays small enough that it cannot be read as a border and never meets the panel's corner radius.

Every grip has its own part (resize-handle-left, resize-handle-bottom-right, and so on, plus resize-handle on all of them). Hit areas and marks are sized separately, so a coarser pointer can get a bigger target without a heavier mark.

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-grip-corner: 20px;          /* the corner squares */
  --ag-ui-grip-edge: 10px;            /* the edge strips */
  --ag-ui-grip-mark-length: 28px;     /* the pill drawn inside them */
  --ag-ui-grip-mark-thickness: 3px;
}

docs.title: Host seams: the SPA story
docs.text:
<ag-ui-chat> is a generic embedding kit; these typed seams let a host feed the agent richer context up front so it explores less. All are framework-free and admin-agnostic.

A router that moves with history.pushState fires no popstate. Where the browser has the Navigation API, the chat follows such a move by itself; elsewhere, call refreshPlace() after each move so the place chip names the new page between runs. The chip's freshness rules are in Where the user is.

routeMap: RouteMap — a manifest of navigable routes ({ id, path, title?, group?, description? }). When set, the element exposes two built-in tools so the agent navigates by intent rather than by exploring:

  • list_routes — read-only; lists the routes.
  • navigate_to_route(route_id, params?) — resolves the id to a path and navigates.

A route path may contain :param segments — e.g. /projects/:id/users/:userId/. navigate_to_route substitutes the path params (URL-encoded) and sends any leftover params as a query string; a missing or empty required path param throws. The resolved shape is the exported RouteWithParams type.

chat.routeMap = [
  { id: "users", path: "/users", title: "Users", description: "Manage user accounts" },
  { id: "billing", path: "/billing", title: "Billing" },
  { id: "user-detail", path: "/projects/:id/users/:userId/", title: "User detail" },
];

getPageMap(): PageMap — a per-run provider returning the current page's compact actionable surface (field names/types/labels, button labels+handles — not values). It is auto-injected into each run's context as a page_map entry (toggle with autoInjectPageMap):

import { pageMapFrom } from "@artooi/agents-web-components";

chat.getPageMap = () => pageMapFrom();

pageMapFrom is the walker the package ships (below); a host with its own model of the page returns that instead, in any shape.

It is recomputed at the top of every tool round, not once per send() — so after the agent acts, the next round already sees the resulting page. Within a round the agent can pull a fresh view at any time with the built-in read_page tool, which is registered whenever this provider is set.

Check that your server reads context at all — pydantic-ai's AG-UI adapter does not. The auto-injected page_map rides in RunAgentInput.context, and an adapter that ignores that field drops it silently: nothing errors, and the model simply never sees the page. On such a backend read_page is the channel that works, and it is the one to rely on. Nothing to configure — just do not assume the injected copy arrived, and if the page map matters to your prompt, put it there server-side or let the agent call read_page.

That leaves one window: the page can move after a round's context was built but before the agent's tool call arrives — the user clicks a link, or presses back. Calls landing in that window are refused with a result telling the agent to call read_page and retry. Most would have missed anyway; the guard exists for the case where a same-named control on the new page matches and the agent would otherwise act on the wrong page without either side noticing. read_page and tools marked x-navigates are exempt. The guard runs in any round that offered read_page, including one you registered yourself, and is inert in a round that did not (no getPageMap, or a place the user withheld), since its result would name a tool the agent does not have.

registerPageState({ name, read, write?, schema? }) — ergonomic sugar over registerTool for SPA app state (Redux/Zustand/signals). It auto-generates a read_<name> (read-only) tool and, when write is supplied, a set_<name> tool stamped x-destructive:

chat.registerPageState({
  name: "cart",
  read: () => store.getState().cart,
  write: ({ items }) => store.dispatch(setCart(items)),
  schema: { type: "object", properties: { items: { type: "array" } } },
});

This is not AG-UI shared state — that is sharedState, below. registerPageState generates two ordinary client tools; the agent reads or writes your store by calling a tool.

sharedState (property) — AG-UI shared state: the protocol's own state channel, sent as RunAgentInput.state on every run and replaced in place when the server streams STATE_SNAPSHOT / STATE_DELTA. Assign to seed it, listen for ag-ui-state to react:

chat.sharedState = { document: "" };

chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-state", (e) => {
  editor.value = e.detail.state.document;   // the agent rewrote it
});

Server-side, a tool mutates ctx.deps.state and returns the snapshot as ToolReturn metadata — pydantic-ai does not emit deltas for you:

@tool(registry)
async def write_document(ctx: RunContext[AgentDeps], body: str) -> ToolReturn:
    """Replace the shared document."""
    ctx.deps.state = {**(ctx.deps.state or {}), "document": body}
    return ToolReturn(
        return_value="written",
        metadata=[StateSnapshotEvent(type=EventType.STATE_SNAPSHOT, snapshot=ctx.deps.state)],
    )

Use this when the agent and the page are editing the same object (a document, a form, a canvas). Because it is the page's object rather than the conversation's, New chat keeps it; a change of user-key clears it. Use registerPageState when the agent should ask for a value or request a change — the tool call is visible in the transcript and can be gated by a confirmation card, which state events cannot.

navigate(path): void (optional) — a host routing callback. This single seam is what distinguishes an SPA from an MPA. When set, navigate_to_route routes client-side (no reload) and the in-memory run loop simply continues — the whole resumable-loop / checkpoint machinery is bypassed. When unset, navigation falls back to window.location and the MPA reload model above applies.

chat.navigate = (path) => router.push(path); // SPA: in-page, no reload
// leave unset for an MPA: window.location + checkpoint/resume

Route map + navigate() and the reload model are the same feature seen from two ends.

ag-ui-run-finished (event) — an interaction has ended, and here is what ran in it. detail: { threadId, tools: readonly ToolRun[], invalidated, outcome } (typed RunFinishedDetail), where each ToolRun is { name, side: "server" | "client" } in settle order. threadId is the thread the run belonged to, which is not always the one on screen: a run that a new chat or a thread switch stopped still reports once its request closes. outcome is how the interaction ended: "completed", "stopped" (Stop, a new chat or a thread switch cut it off, or the server cancelled it; see A run the server stops) or "failed" (the agent reported an error). Ignore an outcome you do not know: more may be added.

This is the seam for a host that renders data the agent can change. A server-side tool writes without your page's knowledge: nothing else the element dispatches implies "something may have moved underneath you", so a page that fetched its data on mount has no reason to refetch and quietly goes stale. Approve a server-side booking on a calendar and the row exists while the calendar keeps showing the week it loaded.

chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-run-finished", (e) => {
  // A "client" tool ran in your own handler, so you already know what it did.
  if (e.detail.tools.some((tool) => tool.side === "server")) {
    void refetchBoard();
  }
});

It fires once per interaction, not once per tool round, and it fires on completion, error and cancellation alike — a partial write is still a write. A capability load (an agent skill activating) is not counted: it moves nothing a host renders.

A run a switch stopped reports outcome: "stopped" whichever thread is on screen when it does, so a listener that marks attention or counts completions tells a cancelled run's late event from a finished one by outcome, not by threadId.

Deferring a switch until the run is over keys on running and data-running, never on this event: it fires for a stopped run too, late, and a stale one can arrive while the next run is live. data-running toggles only for the live run, and there is no running-change event, so watch the attribute:

let queued = null;
const release = () => {
  if (!chat.running && queued !== null) {
    const id = queued;
    queued = null;
    void chat.switchThread(id);
  }
};
new MutationObserver(release).observe(chat, { attributes: true, attributeFilter: ["data-running"] });
myBar.onPick = (id) => {
  if (chat.running) {
    queued = id;
  } else {
    void chat.switchThread(id);
  }
};

sharedState above is the richer channel and this is not a replacement for it — but it is not a substitute the other way round either, because shared state requires the agent to emit STATE_SNAPSHOT, which is not the host's decision to make. Use state when the two ends edit one object; use this when your page owns the data and just needs to know it moved.

ag-ui-custom (event) — the agent sent an AG-UI CUSTOM event. detail: { name, value } (typed CustomAgentDetail), both verbatim and uninterpreted.

chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-custom", (e) => {
  if (e.detail.name === "invalidate") {
    void refetch(e.detail.value);
  }
  // Any other name: no listener, nothing happens. That is the intended outcome.
});

CUSTOM is one of exactly two AG-UI carriers whose payload name is an open string the protocol does not enumerate, and it is the imperative one: something for your page to do. Its sibling ACTIVITY_SNAPSHOT carries transcript content, which is why an activity is materialised into a message, persisted with the thread and replayed on restore, and this is not.

That asymmetry is the rule for choosing between them. Content has a place in the conversation and should replay. An imperative has no place and no meaning once acted on — replaying "refetch the board" on every thread load is a bug, not a feature. If it must survive a reload, it belongs on the other carrier.

The element takes no view of what a name means and forwards every one, so a name it has never heard of reaches you unchanged. A host with no listener for a name simply ignores it, which is the graceful outcome an open field exists for.

ag-ui-invalidate (event) — the agent named resources its write moved. detail: { keys, reason } (typed InvalidateDetail).

One CUSTOM name routed to its own event so you do not have to string-match; every other name still arrives as ag-ui-custom. It fires as each announcement arrives, during the run, and the same keys ride ag-ui-run-finished again at the end as invalidated, de-duplicated.

Do not reload the page on this. The user was probably typing. An agent-triggered reload or a blind refetch into a live form destroys unsaved input, and from their side the page threw their work away on its own. Check first, and offer rather than act:

chat.addEventListener("ag-ui-invalidate", (e) => {
  if (formIsDirty()) {
    showBanner("This data changed. Refresh when you're ready.", e.detail.keys);
    return;
  }
  refetch(e.detail.keys);   // e.detail.keys → ["orders", "orders/42"]
});

Keys are opaque and matching is exact. orders/42 does not imply orders — a prefix rule would be the component guessing at a scheme it does not own, and orders/1 would match orders/11. A server that wants the collection refreshed names it. Your own matching may be hierarchical, because in your vocabulary the scheme is known; that is what TanStack query keys are built for.

Already listening on ag-ui-run-finished? Upgrading is one line, and the else is the whole compatibility story:

if (detail.invalidated.length > 0) refetchOnly(detail.invalidated);
else if (detail.tools.some((t) => t.side === "server")) refetchEverything();
Server Client Result old old coarse refetch, as today new old the CUSTOM event is ignored; coarse refetch still fires old new invalidated is empty; the else branch runs new new precise, and live during the run

Nothing negotiates and nothing handshakes, which is what makes this shippable across repos with independent release cadences.

Note: it reaches the page that started the run, during the run. There is one response stream per run and no channel to anybody else's browser.

docs.title: Reading the page: pageMapFrom
docs.text:
pageMapFrom(root?, options?): PageMap reads the live DOM under root (the document by default) and returns what a model needs to act on it, never what the user typed. It is opt-in: nothing changes for a host that leaves getPageMap unset, or sets its own.

chat.getPageMap = () => pageMapFrom();
chat.getPageMap = () => pageMapFrom(document.querySelector("main"), { limits: { links: 10 } });

Each kind is a key holding a list, left out when empty:

Key Lists Each entry has Cap headings h1-h6, role="heading" level, text 30 landmarks main, nav, aside, search, a top-level header / footer, a named form / section, landmark roles role, name 20 tabs role="tab" name, selected 30 fields inputs, textarea, select, field roles (textbox, combobox, checkbox, slider, ...), contenteditable name (the attribute), type, label, required, disabled 50 buttons button, button inputs, role="button" name, disabled 50 links a[href], role="link" name, href 50 tables table, role="table" / "grid" name, headers (column headers, at most 20) 10 dialogs an open dialog, role="dialog" / "alertdialog" name, modal 5

Past a cap, truncated counts what was left out per kind ({ "links": 12 }); options.limits replaces any cap, and PAGE_MAP_LIMITS holds the defaults. Names and texts are cut at 80 characters. required, disabled appear only when true.

What it never reads. A value rides into the model's context, so the walker reads what the page says about a control, never what is in it:

  • no field's value, and no password or hidden input at all;
  • no aria-valuenow / aria-valuetext (a slider lists its label and role, not its position);
  • no text of a contenteditable region: an editable element is listed as a field (type contenteditable, or its field role), even a heading, tab or header cell, and nothing inside it is listed or read;
  • no text of a textarea, select, input or output, nor of anything not rendered (hidden, display: none, visibility: hidden, aria-hidden="true"), marked data-agent-ignore, or of this package's elements (ag-ui-*, their shadow roots included). This holds wherever a name or text comes from: an element's own content, a <label> wrapping its control, a table's header cells, or an aria-labelledby reference, so a reference that points at an editable region, a textarea or a select names nothing (and a reference to a hidden element names nothing either);
  • no option text, so neither the selected option nor the choices are listed;
  • no link's query string or fragment: href is the path, with the origin when it is another site, cut at 80 characters, and for a scheme other than http: / https: (mailto:, tel:, javascript:, data:) the scheme alone;
  • nothing inside a field: a listbox, an editable region or any other field ends the walk;
  • a placeholder only as the label of last resort, after aria-labelledby, aria-label, the field's <label>s and title, since it is author text.

Text the page itself writes is read as it is: a heading or label that prints user data ("Signed in as ...") reaches the model like any other text. Mark such a region data-agent-ignore.

Inside an <svg>, only its links are listed: an <a> with an href or xlink:href (or with role="link"), under the same rules for href as any link. Its name comes from aria-labelledby, aria-label, title or its text, not from a <title> child. Other SVG elements are not listed, whatever role they carry, while the HTML in a <foreignObject> is listed as anywhere else. An SVG's text counts toward the name of the element around it (never its <script> or <style>). The handle of an SVG link resolves to an SVGElement, which has no click(): clickElement and pressButton dispatch the click event instead, so a host tool of its own should do the same.

What it skips. The subtree of every element of this package (ag-ui-*, so the chat never lists itself), of anything marked data-agent-ignore, and of anything hidden (hidden, display: none, visibility: hidden), inert or aria-hidden="true". It walks open shadow roots of your components; a closed one is unreachable by design.

Handles. Each listed element is stamped data-agent-handle="n", and its entry carries the selector for it, [data-agent-handle="n"], which the default resolvePageTarget resolves, so scroll_to and drag_and_drop act on it with no host code. A handle is kept across reads while its element is listed, and a clone that carries the same stamp gets a new one. Numbers only grow while the document lives: the number of an element that was removed, hidden or not listed is never given to another, so a handle kept from an earlier read does not come to name a new element. A page load starts again from the stamps it finds, and a copy of an element carries its stamp until the next read.

The default resolver is resolvePageMapHandle: document.querySelector first, and only when that misses and the target is exactly a handle of this form, a search of the open shadow roots under the document (skipping this package's own elements), so a handle the walker stamped inside a component resolves too. Any other selector resolves in the light DOM alone, as before. A host that overrides resolvePageTarget and still wants handles to resolve falls back to it:

import { resolvePageMapHandle } from "@artooi/agents-web-components";

chat.resolvePageTarget = (target) => myPageMap.elementFor(target) ?? resolvePageMapHandle(target);

docs.title: Where the user is: the place chip
docs.text:
The composer can say where in your app the user is writing from: a chip in its tool row, between the attach and voice controls and Send, naming the page, tab or record on screen. The same read is sent to the agent as one context entry, so the place the user sees is the place the agent is told.

getPlace: () => Place | null returns a Place: { label, detail?, icon?, href? }. The chip draws the label, the detail after a dot, and the icon (an image URL; a pin when absent). The agent gets a place context entry whose value is the JSON of the label, detail and href; the icon is never sent. The href identifies the place; without one, the label and detail do.

chat.getPlace = () => ({
  label: `Order #${order.number}`,
  detail: "Orders",
  href: location.pathname,
});
  • With no getPlace, a route map stands in. The routeMap route whose path matches location.pathname names the place: its title (else its id) as the label, its group as the detail, and the path as the href. A host with a route map gets the chip without writing anything. With neither, no chip is drawn and nothing is sent; set getPlace = () => null to opt a route-mapped host out.
  • When it is read. Before every tool round, so an agent that navigates mid-run is told the new page on its next round; and on connect, on expand, when the composer gains focus, on popstate and hashchange, on the Navigation API's currententrychange where the browser has it (which a pushState move fires), and when the conversation on screen changes (switchThread, the drawer, newChat): the chip always names the live page, never the page a thread started on. Between runs it shows the last read. In a browser without the Navigation API a single-page app calls refreshPlace() after its router moves, since pushState fires no other event.
  • The entry rides after your getContext. It is appended to whatever getContext returns, so a host that replaces getContext still sends it.
  • The eye toggle withholds it. Pressing it leaves the chip in place, dashed and struck through (data-excluded on the place part), and the next round sends no place entry. It withholds the page too: that round also drops the page_map entry, whatever getContext returned, and does not offer read_page. Tools you register yourself, such as registerPageState's, stay as you registered them. The choice holds while the same place is read, lapses when a different place is read, is not persisted, and cannot be lifted by the host.
  • Placement. The same position in every placement, on a phone and in the greeting layout; the label truncates with an ellipsis before it can push Send off the row, and the chip's title carries it in full. Nothing shows while the panel is collapsed. The chip is separate from the above-composer slot, and filling the slot never hides it.
  • Styling and words. Parts place, place-icon, place-label, place-detail and place-toggle; the colours come from the existing tokens. The tooltip and the toggle's labels are the placeShared and placeWithheld (token {label}), placeStopSharing and placeShareAgain strings.

docs.title: Internationalization (i18n)
docs.text:
Every user-facing string — labels, placeholders, aria-labels, and title tooltips — is read from a flat UiStrings table, so a non-English host can translate the widget without forking it. Override any subset; the rest fall back to the English defaults. Two equivalent seams:

// As a property (merged over the defaults):
chat.strings = { send: "Senden", inputPlaceholder: "Frag mich…", stop: "Stopp" };

<!-- Or inline, as JSON (the property wins key-by-key when both are set): -->
<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-strings='{"send": "Senden", "inputPlaceholder": "Frag mich…"}'></ag-ui-chat>

Set strings / data-strings before the element connects (they resolve on mount). A few keys are templates carrying {token} placeholders the widget fills in — e.g. minutesAgo ("{n}m ago"), confirmRun ("Run “{tool}”?"), tooLarge ("Too large (max {size})"). Keep the token verbatim when translating. The full key list and English defaults live in src/ui/ui_strings.ts (exported as DEFAULT_UI_STRINGS); mergeUiStrings is exported too if you want to compute a complete table yourself. The read-only uiStrings property is the table the element draws with once connected (defaults, then data-strings, then strings).

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
npm install @artooi/agents-web-components

The package ships two builds (see package.json exports):

Entry What it is When to use @artooi/agents-web-components ESM library build; @ag-ui/* stay external You bundle the app yourself (Vite, webpack, esbuild) and want to dedupe @ag-ui/*. @artooi/agents-web-components/chat The same library build's <ag-ui-chat> entry: AgUiChat and defineChat Beside the root entry; the two share one module instance, so import from both freely. @artooi/agents-web-components/threads <ag-ui-threads>, the conversation list for your own bar or rail: AgUiThreads and defineThreads Beside ./chat, when you draw the list of conversations yourself. @artooi/agents-web-components/threads/bundle The same entry as a vendored file, minified, inlining none of the element Beside /bundle with no build step; the main bundle does not carry the list. @artooi/agents-web-components/inbox <ag-ui-inbox>, what waits on the user across agents, as a navbar badge or a list: AgUiInbox and defineInbox Beside ./chat and an <ag-ui-agents> provider. @artooi/agents-web-components/inbox/bundle The same entry as a vendored file, minified, inlining none of the element or the provider Beside /bundle with no build step; the main bundle does not carry the inbox. @artooi/agents-web-components/routines <ag-ui-routines>, the routines editor as an element of its own: AgUiRoutines and defineRoutines When the routines live on a page or in a rail of their own, away from the chat. @artooi/agents-web-components/routines/bundle The same entry as a vendored file, minified, inlining none of the chat or the provider Beside /bundle, or alone, with no build step. @artooi/agents-web-components/skills <ag-ui-skills>, the stored-skill editor as an element of its own: AgUiSkills and defineSkills When the skills live on a page of their own, away from the chat. @artooi/agents-web-components/skills/bundle The same entry as a vendored file, minified, inlining none of the chat or the provider Beside /bundle, or alone, with no build step. @artooi/agents-web-components/bundle ESM bundle with @ag-ui/* inlined, minified Drop in via a single <script type="module"> with no build step.

docs.title: The vendored-bundle story
docs.text: The /bundle entry inlines every dependency into one self-contained ESM file (dist/agents-web-components.bundle.js). This is the artefact intended for vendoring: a host that can't (or won't) run a JS build — for example a Django app — copies the built bundle into its static/ directory and serves it directly. django-admin-agent re-vendors a pinned built bundle on every release. For SPA hosts that already have a bundler, import the bare package name instead so @ag-ui/client / @ag-ui/core are deduped against the rest of your app.

docs.title: Types for a vendoring TypeScript host
docs.text:
Beside the bundle the package ships dist/agents-web-components.bundle.d.ts, one self-contained declaration file for everything the bundle exports. The @ag-ui/core, @ag-ui/client, dompurify and rxjs types it needs are inlined into it, as their code is inlined into the bundle, so a TypeScript host that vendors needs nothing else: copy both files into the same directory and import the .js path.

// static/vendor/ holds agents-web-components.bundle.js and agents-web-components.bundle.d.ts
