With django-ag-ui 0.91.0 and a skill policy that defines scope(request, skill), each editor entry carries scope, and the row draws a badge after the skill's name: Personal for "personal", Company for "shared". An entry without scope (an older server, or a policy without the method) draws no badge, as before. The badge is the part skill-scope, with the value in data-scope, so a host can style each scope:

ag-ui-chat::part(skill-scope) { color: var(--ag-ui-muted); }

The words are strings keyed skillScope:<value>. Override the two the component knows, or name a label for a scope your own policy returns; a scope with no label draws no badge, since its raw value may be an internal name rather than words for a user. The same keys work on <ag-ui-skills>'s strings:

chat.strings = {
  "skillScope:shared": "Acme",
  "skillScope:team": "Team",
};

Writes are CSRF-checked by default on the server, and each one sends headers and getHeaders() as read at that moment, so a getHeaders returning the current CSRF token is all a Django host needs:

chat.getHeaders = () => ({ "X-CSRFToken": readCookie("csrftoken") });

The palette catches up without a reload: after each save from the editor, on every change of user-key, and whenever a run sends django-ag-ui's ag_ui.skills_changed CUSTOM event (still forwarded to the page as ag-ui-custom). A user-key handover also closes the editor and drops what it held, the previous principal's skill bodies included.

docs.title: Routines
docs.text:
django-ag-ui (0.86.0 on, with routine_model=) serves a caller's routines: prompts the agent runs on a schedule. Point data-routines-url at that mount's routines/ route and the header gains a Routines button that opens them in the full-panel view:

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-routines-url="/agent/routines/" data-threads-url="/agent/threads/"></ag-ui-chat>

Each row says its schedule in words (in the routine's own timezone, named when it is not the viewer's), its next run (or why it is paused) and its last result, which opens that run's thread. Pause or Resume and Run now act on the row. The view's bar adds a routine, and a row opens its form: name, prompt, a weekly or every-few-hours schedule, the timezone, and the tools each run may use without asking, offered from the server's grantable list. A destructive tool is marked, and granting it asks first, naming it destructive; the grant is then sent in confirmDestructive on every save, as the server requires. Make this a routine, at the foot of the list, in the header's More menu once a prompt is on screen, and as makeRoutine(), opens the form with the conversation's own prompts as the routine's.

Writes are JSON and carry getHeaders(), so a CSRF header reaches them as it reaches the skill editor. With data-threads-url on the same mount, a thread a routine started carries a badge with the routine's name in the thread list. openRoutines() and closeRoutines() open and close the view; a principal change closes it.

The skill editor and routines can also stand on the page as elements of their own; see The editors on a page of their own.

docs.title: The time and timezone fields
docs.text:
The form's time is two selects, the hour (00 to 23) and the minute in steps of five, drawn by the panel's tokens rather than the browser's time popup, and announced as one group named by the At caption. data-routine-minute-step changes the step; a routine whose minute is off the step keeps its exact minute as an option of its own, never rounded. The timezone is a text input suggesting the browser's IANA zones (Intl.supportedValuesOf("timeZone")), set to the viewer's zone on a new routine; an unknown zone is refused by the server, in its words.

Either field can be replaced by a control of your own, slotted on the element:

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-routines-url="/agent/routines/">
  <select slot="routine-time" aria-label="Run at">
    <option>07:00</option><option>08:00</option><option>18:00</option>
  </select>
  <select slot="routine-timezone" aria-label="Timezone">
    <option>UTC</option><option>Europe/Paris</option>
  </select>
</ag-ui-chat>
Slot Value routine-time HH:MM, 24-hour, as the wire carries it routine-timezone An IANA zone name

The contract is a value, not a type: any element with a string value property. When the form opens a routine it sets the control's value to the routine's (once per opening, so a re-render of your control does not overwrite a choice in progress), and on save it reads value. Nothing listens for change. A <select> that has no option for the routine's value shows nothing chosen, so offer every value your routines can hold. The form's caption cannot name a slotted control across the shadow boundary: give yours its own aria-label. The slotted controls are yours to style; the built-in fields stay in the form as the slots' fallback content.

docs.title: Theming, density, and placement
docs.text:
The chat shell is styled inside its Shadow DOM and exposes a large set of --ag-ui-* CSS custom properties (colors, status, surface, spacing, layout), so you theme it from outside without piercing the shadow boundary. Set them anywhere above the element and they inherit in — on the element itself, on a wrapper, or on :root for a whole page. The closest declaration wins, the way any inherited CSS property behaves:

/* All three work. The most specific one that applies wins. */
:root      { --ag-ui-accent: #4f46e5; }  /* whole page */
.chat-dock { --ag-ui-accent: #0f766e; }  /* one region */
ag-ui-chat { --ag-ui-accent: #b91c1c; }  /* one widget */

Until 0.20.x the defaults were declared on :host, which set them on the element — and an element's own value beats anything inherited from an ancestor, so only the ag-ui-chat { … } form did anything and the wrapper form silently did nothing. The defaults now sit behind an internal alias, so all three forms work.

A few of the knobs, at Quiet's light values:

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-accent: #232326;        /* #f0f0f2 in the dark scheme */
  --ag-ui-bg: #ffffff;            /* #161618 */
  --ag-ui-fg: #1b1b1d;            /* #ececee */
  --ag-ui-radius: 12px;
  --ag-ui-header-btn-size: 30px;  /* the header's controls; 44px on touch */
  --ag-ui-header-gap: 4px;

  /* What is drawn on top of the accent and danger fills. Unset, the one on
     the accent is white or black by the accent's luminance (see Text on the
     accent below); set it to pin a colour of your own. */
  --ag-ui-on-accent: #ffffff;
  --ag-ui-on-danger: #ffffff;

  /* Layout */
  --ag-ui-width: 380px;
  --ag-ui-height: 560px;
  --ag-ui-inset: auto 24px 24px auto;
  --ag-ui-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.05), 0 12px 32px -16px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.22);
}

--ag-ui-radius is the theme's corner radius. It rounds the panel's frame and the corners inside the panel that have no radius of their own: the answer well, the conversation list's New chat button and filter field, and the Undo on a run notice. The frame is the exception where it meets the edge of the window. page and sidebar draw it square, and so does every placement but embedded on a small viewport, while the corners inside keep the theme's radius, since none of them meets that edge. --ag-ui-panel-radius sets the frame on its own, in any placement. Each theme gives the floating frame a radius of its own (--ag-ui-frame-radius: 14px in Quiet against 12px inside), and a host's --ag-ui-radius still sets both.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
theme is up to two words, in any order, matched as words (~=):

theme = [name] [scheme]
name   = quiet | soft | ledger | classic | <a word of your own>
scheme = light | dark | auto            default: light
Value Result (absent) Quiet, light dark Quiet, dark auto Quiet, following the system's prefers-color-scheme soft, soft dark, ledger auto that theme in that scheme classic, classic dark the look from before themes, for a host that pins it acme a word the component does not ship adds no rules, so this is Quiet, ready for your [theme~="acme"] CSS soft acme starts from Soft; your [theme~="acme"] rules layer on top

The built-in themes:

Theme Look quiet The default. Neutral graphite on white, no bubble for the agent's turn, hairlines, status as an icon. Set one brand accent and the user's turn, the send button and the links follow it. soft Rounded and tinted: surfaces mixed from the accent, pill chips, a deep frame shadow. Violet by default. ledger Dense and editorial: paper and ink, square corners, serif for what the agent says and monospace for the chrome. classic The look before themes: the indigo header, the accent user bubble, the status pill and the round launcher. Pin it to keep that look.

The default scheme is light, not auto, because the widget sits on your page and only you know that page's scheme. A light admin screen on a machine in dark mode would otherwise get a dark panel on a white page. If your page follows the system, say auto.

Each theme is three seeds, --ag-ui-bg, --ag-ui-fg and --ag-ui-accent, each declared with light-dark() so the scheme word picks the half. Every other colour is mixed from them with color-mix(in oklch, ...) -- hover, borders, the secondary text inks, washes, the user's turn (the accent at 12% over the background) -- and every derived value still reads its own public token first, so each stays an override point. The tokens the themes add:

  • Inks and lines: --ag-ui-ink-2, --ag-ui-ink-3, --ag-ui-line, --ag-ui-line-strong.
  • Surfaces: --ag-ui-wash, --ag-ui-accent-ink, --ag-ui-tint, --ag-ui-tint-2.
  • Type: --ag-ui-text-xs, --ag-ui-text-sm, --ag-ui-text-md, --ag-ui-text-lg, --ag-ui-leading, --ag-ui-serif.
  • Frame: --ag-ui-frame-radius, --ag-ui-frame-shadow. These are what a theme sets for the frame; --ag-ui-panel-radius and --ag-ui-shadow stay the final say, and are what a docked placement squares or flattens.
  • Charts: --ag-ui-chart-1 to --ag-ui-chart-6. A host's value beats the theme's.
  • Status marks: --ag-ui-ico-check, --ag-ui-ico-error, --ag-ui-ico-declined, mask images drawn in the state's colour, and --ag-ui-ico-chevron, the step group's disclosure chevron.
  • Focus: --ag-ui-ring, the step group head's focus outline. Unset, it is two parts accent to three parts ink (--ag-ui-fg), which holds 3:1 against the panel for any accent.

The font is part of the theme: Quiet, Soft and Ledger set their own stack (Inter, then the system UI font), and Classic inherits the page's font as the component always did. To take the page's font under any theme, set --ag-ui-font to the page's family, or to the page's own font token:

ag-ui-chat { --ag-ui-font: var(--body-font); }   /* or the family itself */

--ag-ui-font: inherit does not do this. A CSS-wide keyword in a custom property applies to the custom property itself, so it takes the --ag-ui-font of the parent, which nothing sets, and the theme's stack wins.

docs.title: Text on the accent
docs.text:
--ag-ui-on-accent, unless you set it, is picked from the accent's own luminance: white on an accent darker than WCAG relative luminance 0.179, black on a lighter one, which is the better of the two on every colour (never under 4.58:1). It is computed with relative colour syntax with channel arithmetic, behind @supports for that exact expression: Chrome 119, Firefox 128, Safari 18.

The fallback. Two browsers at or above the floor cannot compute it: Firefox 120 to 127, which lack relative colour syntax, and Safari 17.5 and 17.6, which shipped an earlier draft that rejects this expression. They keep a fixed colour per theme instead:

Theme Without relative colour syntax quiet, soft, ledger the scheme's: white in the light scheme, near-black (#111111) in the dark one classic, code white in both schemes, the colour they always drew

On every built-in accent but code's the fixed colour is on the same side as the computed one, so those browsers see the same contrast. On code's green the computed pick is black (8.3:1) and the fallback white (2.5:1), as it always was. What they miss is the correction for a host's accent: a mid-tone brand accent can fall under 4.5:1 there, under any theme. If you support those browsers and set a mid-tone accent, set --ag-ui-on-accent yourself. There is no script path.

docs.title: Keeping a brand accent on the header
docs.text:
Quiet draws the header, the launcher and the tool names in the panel's own colours, so a host that sets only --ag-ui-accent gets a neutral header. To put the accent back without leaving Quiet, set the surfaces to the accent and the text on them to a colour that reads on it. The same recipe holds under every other theme:

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-header-bg: #3d5afe;
  --ag-ui-header-fg: #ffffff;
  --ag-ui-launcher-bg: #3d5afe;
  --ag-ui-launcher-fg: #ffffff;
  --ag-ui-tool-fg: #3d5afe;
}
  • The header buttons follow --ag-ui-header-fg, under every theme. Unset, each theme draws them its own way at 0.85 opacity: Quiet, Soft and Ledger in their third ink, Classic and Code in the header text, each on its own hover square. Once you set the header text they draw in it at full opacity, and the hover square is the opposite of that text at about a fifth (a darker square under white text, a lighter one under dark text), so a hovered button reads at least what your header pair reads. A theme word of your own starts from Quiet, so it holds there too. No ::part(header-button) rule is needed. The opposite is computed with relative colour syntax; the browsers without it (see the fallback above) mix the square from the text itself, which on a mid-tone header can take the hovered glyph under your pair (white on #3d5afe: 3.75:1).
  • --ag-ui-header-btn-hover sets the hover square outright under every theme, whether or not the header text is set, and is drawn exactly as given. For a square that lightens under white text instead, at the cost of contrast on a mid-tone header:

ag-ui-chat { --ag-ui-header-btn-hover: color-mix(in srgb, #ffffff 18%, transparent); }
- --ag-ui-tool-fg colours every tool call, in a step group as well as in the card displays. Unset, a grouped call is drawn in the second ink (--ag-ui-ink-2) under every theme. - Pick the pair yourself: --ag-ui-header-fg is not derived from the header colour the way --ag-ui-on-accent is from the accent.

docs.title: Overriding a theme, lightest layer first
docs.text: Four layers, each documented and each lighter than the next. Reach for the first one that does the job.

docs.title: (a) Tokens
docs.text:
Any --ag-ui-* token, on the element or any ancestor, as above. Per theme, from your own CSS:

body { --ag-ui-accent: #0f766e; }          /* accent only: the rest follows */
ag-ui-chat[theme~="soft"] { --ag-ui-accent: #c2410c; --ag-ui-frame-radius: 12px; }

A page rule always beats the theme's own value, because the theme only ever sets the private alias behind the public token.

docs.title: (b) Parts
docs.text:
::part() reaches the structural elements, as listed in Parts and slots:

ag-ui-chat::part(header) { background: linear-gradient(#f2f7f6, transparent); }

docs.title: (c) A theme of your own
docs.text:
Name it, and style the name. An unknown word adds no built-in rules, so it starts from Quiet (or from the built-in theme beside it):

<ag-ui-chat theme="acme dark"></ag-ui-chat>

ag-ui-chat[theme~="acme"] {
  --ag-ui-bg: light-dark(#fbfaf7, #10161c);
  --ag-ui-fg: light-dark(#14212b, #e4ebf0);
  --ag-ui-accent: light-dark(#0b5cad, #6cb2ff);
  --ag-ui-frame-radius: 4px;
}

Use light-dark() in the seeds and the scheme word, and the theme toggle, work for your theme too.

docs.title: (d) extraStyles: the last mile
docs.text:
Unstable. extraStyles reaches the class names inside the shadow root, and those are not a public API: they may change in any minor release. Layers (a) to (c) are the supported ones; use this for what they cannot reach, and expect to revisit it on upgrade.

const sheet = new CSSStyleSheet();
sheet.replaceSync(`.message--assistant { padding: 10px 12px; border-radius: 10px; }`);
chat.extraStyles = [sheet];
  • extraStyles: readonly CSSStyleSheet[], per element, default []. Two elements can carry different sheets.
  • Adopted after the built-in sheet, so a rule of equal specificity wins.
  • Setting it re-adopts at once. The array is copied, so changing the one you passed does nothing until you set it again; changing a sheet's rules does apply, since the sheet itself is shared.
  • Constructed sheets are not subject to style-src, so this works under the same strict CSP as the built-in sheet. There is no string form and no <style> injection.

docs.title: Small viewports
docs.text:
At 600px wide and below every placement but embedded becomes one full-bleed shape: edge to edge, no radius, no shadow, no resize grips. A phone is not an eighth placement — it is an override that collapses the others onto one of them. The host picked a placement for the desktop it was designing, and a 380x560 panel with a 24px margin is not a smaller version of that decision, it is most of the screen with a frame drawn round it.

embedded is left alone deliberately: it sits in a box you sized and placed, and only you know whether that column should become the whole screen.

The greeting layout changes shape here too, and it is the one part of this that embedded gets as well, because it moves nothing about the box you placed: an empty conversation keeps its composer at the foot of the panel, with the starters against it and the greeting over the space above them, instead of centring all three together.

The corner placements still rest at their launcher, so a full-bleed panel is something the user opens rather than something they are given.

To keep your desktop layout at every width, set data-small-viewport="off". That exists because the trigger is the one part of this you cannot reach: every value the override sets is a --ag-ui-* token you can re-state, but a media query cannot read a custom property, so the breakpoint itself is a literal.

A size or inset token set at every width restates the phone shape too. The phone block reads --ag-ui-inset, --ag-ui-width, --ag-ui-height and --ag-ui-max-height before it falls back to the full-bleed values, so a host rule such as the one below keeps its 420x640 panel with a 24px margin on a phone, and the panel runs off the screen's left edge. Put the desktop sizes above the breakpoint and the phone shape needs nothing:

/* Wrong on a phone: the tokens apply at every width. */
ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-inset: auto 24px 24px auto;
  --ag-ui-width: 420px;
  --ag-ui-height: 640px;
  --ag-ui-max-height: 80vh;
}

/* Right: desktop only. At 600px and below the panel is full-bleed with no reset. */
@media (min-width: 601px) {
  ag-ui-chat {
    --ag-ui-inset: auto 24px 24px auto;
    --ag-ui-width: 420px;
    --ag-ui-height: 640px;
    --ag-ui-max-height: 80vh;
  }
}

Setting the tokens at every width stays right for a host that wants a non-full-bleed phone panel, a bottom sheet for example. The size a user dragged is a separate matter; see Sizes, keyboard, and parts for its precedence.

The breakpoint is a width rather than a pointer test, and that is on purpose: a touch laptop is coarse-pointered and wide, a narrow desktop window is fine-pointered and small. Width decides the layout; the pointer decides which controls make sense.

docs.title: The conversation list
docs.text:
The chat-history list slides over the transcript at every width and under every placement, a full page included. Opening it moves nothing underneath: the conversation, the centred greeting and the composer are exactly where they were. While it is open it is a modal dialog: focus moves into it, Tab stays inside it, and Escape, its close control or a click on the backdrop beside it closes it and returns focus to where it was. openThreads() and closeThreads() do the same from your own chrome.

The list also grows a filter once there are eight or more conversations in it — above that a search box is worth having, below it it is a control asking to be used on a list you can already read in one glance. It matches the title and the preview, because the title is often the model's one-line summary and the phrase you remember is as likely to be inside the conversation as on it, and it filters what the drawer already holds rather than going back to the server for a list that is already in memory. data-threads-search="always" shows it over any list and "never" hides it, for a host whose lists are always short or always long.

The rows are grouped by when they were last active: Today, Previous 7 days and Older, counted from local midnight. A group with no rows is not drawn, and a list that falls in one group draws no heading at all. A conversation with no readable date goes under Older. A filtered list keeps its groups. The headings are not in the Tab order, are styled as ::part(drawer-group-label), and take their text from the threadsToday, threadsPreviousWeek and threadsOlder strings. Every drawer has them: the slide-over, the bar's popover and the popover beside your own button.

docs.title: Reserving the space your own chrome occupies
docs.text:
A fixed placement covers the viewport it is given, and it does not know about your sticky header. Tell it which edges are already spent and every placement does its own arithmetic:

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-viewport-inset-top: 64px;    /* your nav bar */
}

page and full inset by all four edges; sidebar and side by three, leaving the docked edge free; floating adds them to its own margins. The heights follow on their own — that is the point of these rather than restating --ag-ui-inset per placement, which leaves you to keep --ag-ui-height and --ag-ui-max-height in step by hand and overflows the panel off the bottom of the screen the one time you forget.

Four longhands rather than one shorthand because a custom property is a token stream and CSS cannot index one; the height arithmetic needs the vertical pair on its own. Any CSS length works — px, rem, env(safe-area-inset-*), or a calc() combining them; the widget reads the resolved value rather than the text you wrote, so the number it clamps against is the one the stylesheet uses:

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-viewport-inset-top: env(safe-area-inset-top);
  --ag-ui-viewport-inset-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom);
}

If your chrome changes height — a bar that wraps at narrow widths — measure it and publish the value, since no CSS length tracks it:

new ResizeObserver(() => {
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--bar-h", `${bar.offsetHeight}px`);
}).observe(bar);

ag-ui-chat { --ag-ui-viewport-inset-top: var(--bar-h, 0px); }

--ag-ui-edge-gutter (default 24px) is the gap a resting floating panel keeps between itself and that box. The size cap subtracts the same one, so a panel grown to its limit reaches the far edge of the usable box and no further — set it to 0 for a panel flush against the corner.

--ag-ui-anchor-gap (default 8px) is the gap between the panel and the button it rises from under collapse-to="none"; see Collapsing to a bottom bar.

--ag-ui-keyboard-inset overrides the lift an on-screen keyboard earns. The widget measures the hidden band and publishes it as --ag-ui-visual-viewport-inset-bottom; state this one instead to outrank that measurement, or set it to 0px to opt out of the lift entirely.

--ag-ui-keyboard-inset-top does the same at the top. To show a field a keyboard would cover, a mobile browser pans the visible area down the page, and a panel anchored to the screen (page, full, side, sidebar, and at phone width the corner placements too) moves down with it. An embedded panel renders in your own box rather than against the screen, so it does not move at any width. The widget publishes the pan as --ag-ui-visual-viewport-inset-top, and the panel moves by as much of it as goes past your --ag-ui-viewport-inset-top, since the pan scrolls a reserved bar away with the page. State --ag-ui-keyboard-inset-top to outrank that distance, or 0px to keep the panel below your reserved top.

--ag-ui-viewport-height and --ag-ui-viewport-width state the usable box outright, for the case where no viewport-percentage length describes it. An on-screen keyboard is the one that matters: it changes neither vh nor dvh nor svh on any current mobile browser, so a full-bleed panel has to be told the visual viewport's height rather than deriving it. The widget does that itself; where it has nothing to report, the panel falls back to 100dvh rather than 100vh, because iOS Safari resolves vh to the screen with its bars collapsed and a panel sized from it runs under them.

Marks are variables too, so one vocabulary covers a re-theme rather than leaving half the transcript in the built-in set: --ag-ui-tool-icon-done / -error / -declined for tool status, and --ag-ui-disclosure-collapsed / --ag-ui-disclosure-expanded for every expandable row.

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-disclosure-collapsed: "+";
  --ag-ui-disclosure-expanded: "-";
}

docs.title: Where to put the variables
docs.text:
There is one vocabulary — the --ag-ui-* names above — and it works from any ancestor. What differs is only which declaration wins, and that is ordinary CSS inheritance:

/* A whole page or design-system scope. */
:root { --ag-ui-accent: var(--brand-600); --ag-ui-radius: 4px; }

/* One region — the widget picks this up through the wrapper. */
aside.support-dock { --ag-ui-accent: #0f766e; }

/* One widget. Beats both of the above, because it targets the element. */
ag-ui-chat#support { --ag-ui-accent: #b91c1c; }

/* Set at runtime with el.style.setProperty(...) — an inline style beats all of the above. */

Two that do not work:

/* ::part() reaches structural elements, not variables — a custom property set
   here applies to that part's own subtree, not to the whole shell. */
ag-ui-chat::part(panel) { --ag-ui-accent: #b91c1c; }

/* The internal --_* aliases are private and unversioned; they are renamed
   without notice. Always set the public --ag-ui-* name. */
ag-ui-chat { --_accent: #b91c1c; }

The preset attributes below sit underneath anything you declare: a theme="dark" widget still honours an explicit --ag-ui-bg from your CSS, so you can adopt a preset and correct one token rather than re-declaring the whole palette.

--ag-ui-accent reaches further than the widget: it also colours the rings the DOM driver draws on your page. Each primitive reads it from the computed style of the element it is about to touch, so setting it on :root (or on any ancestor of the elements the agent drives) themes the highlights too. Without it they fall back to the package indigo.

For the common cases there are three CSS-reactive preset attributes (no JS API), so you don't have to hand-tune the variables:

  • theme — a theme name and a scheme; see Themes.
  • density — comfortable (default) / compact.
  • placement — floating (default) / sidebar / page / embedded. embedded drops the fixed positioning and z-index so the widget sits in normal document flow; page is a full-screen centred reading column for a route of its own.

Four, because those are the four shapes that differ structurally: a corner panel, a docked rail, a surface that owns the screen, and a thing in your layout. Three older values -- bottom-left, side and full -- still parse and still work, and are no longer documented: each is a variant of one of the four rather than a shape of its own. full is page with --ag-ui-content-max-width: none, bottom-left is floating with a different --ag-ui-inset, and side is sidebar that collapses to the floating launcher instead of an edge rail. Nothing warns and nothing breaks; there is simply less to choose between.

embedded fills the box your page gives it, so give it one. It is the placement app-shell layouts reach for, and a grid or flex item defaults to min-height: auto — which lets a growing transcript push the composer off the bottom of the window instead of scrolling inside the panel. The fix belongs to the containing element, not to the widget:

.assistant-pane { min-height: 0; overflow: hidden; }   /* the box the element is given */

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" theme="dark" density="compact" placement="sidebar"></ag-ui-chat>

See src/ui/shell/token_styles.ts for the full variable list and src/ui/placement/ for the placement presets. The demo/ (make demo) has a scenario for each: placements, themes and tokens, answers and reasoning, tool display, and the rest, each switched live on its own page.

The demo server binds every interface and prints the addresses this machine can be reached on, so you can open the demo on a phone — which is the only way to see the small-viewport layout with a real on-screen keyboard rather than a resized desktop window. HOST=127.0.0.1 keeps it to this machine.

docs.title: Parts and slots
docs.text:
For styling beyond the --ag-ui-* variables, every structural element exposes a part so you can reach it from outside the Shadow DOM with ::part() — no shadow piercing. The part names are public API (additions are non-breaking; renames are breaking):

ag-ui-chat::part(panel)   { border-radius: 0; }
ag-ui-chat::part(header)  { background: #111; }
ag-ui-chat::part(send)    { text-transform: uppercase; }
ag-ui-chat::part(tool-card) { font-family: var(--my-mono); }

Every part, by the feature it belongs to. Spelled out rather than abbreviated: the list used to read tool-card plus -icon / -name, which is compact and is also how an entire feature went missing from it for two releases. Hiding ::part(header) hides the controls inside it. The history, checkpoints, new-chat, theme and collapse buttons are all children of the header, so a host that renders its own title bar and does ag-ui-chat::part(header) { display: none } loses thread switching entirely. Every one of them has an imperative equivalent, so your own chrome can drive them:

Control Method History drawer chat.openThreads() Checkpoints panel chat.openCheckpoints() New chat chat.newChat() Collapse chat.toggleCollapsed() / chat.setCollapsed(bool) Theme toggle chat.toggleTheme() 
myHeaderButton.onclick = () => chat.openThreads();

The built-in buttons call exactly these methods, so the two routes cannot drift. If you only want to restyle the header, prefer ::part(header) styling or the header-actions slot over hiding it.

To drop single controls instead, hide their parts: ag-ui-chat::part(history-button), ag-ui-chat::part(new-button) { display: none }. display: none removes them from the accessibility tree and the tab order as well.

Coarse slots let you replace whole regions with your own markup (project light-DOM children with a matching slot=):

Slot Where icon A header brand icon, before the title. header-actions Extra controls between the title and the built-in buttons. greeting The greeting's text, above the empty state, where the greeting layout is on. Replaces the text only; empty and the starters still render beneath it. empty The empty-state shown before any message. above-composer Directly above the composer, below the skill chips, hint, queued turns and attachment tray. Takes no space when empty, and moves with the composer in the greeting layout. footer Below the composer. launcher The collapsed widget's mark — the floating launcher, or the sidebar rail. icon-send / icon-stop The composer button's two glyphs (idle and mid-run). icon-attach / icon-voice The paperclip and mic glyphs. icon-history / icon-checkpoints / icon-new / icon-maximize / icon-collapse The header controls' glyphs. A slotted icon-collapse wins over data-collapse-icon. 
<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/">
  <img slot="icon" src="/logo.svg" alt="" />
  <button slot="header-actions" onclick="openHelp()">?</button>
</ag-ui-chat>

docs.title: Header and launcher icon
docs.text:
Give the header a brand icon with either the icon slot (any markup) or the data-icon-url convenience attribute (an <img>); the slot wins when both are set, and with neither the header stays icon-less. The same icon seam feeds the collapsed sidebar rail. Size it via --ag-ui-icon-size (default 22px) and round it with --ag-ui-icon-radius (default 4px).

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-icon-url="/logo.png"></ag-ui-chat>

docs.title: Sidebar placement
docs.text:
placement="sidebar" is a full-height docked panel that slides open/closed and collapses to a slim icon rail rather than the floating launcher — the same element, shaped by the placement. It docks right by default; data-side="left" docks it left. The panel slides out through the edge it docks against. Collapse state reuses the collapsed attribute (persisted per-tab), and the rail carries aria-expanded. The slide honours prefers-reduced-motion.

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" placement="sidebar" data-side="left"></ag-ui-chat>

It overlays the page by default (no host-layout coupling). To make the host content reflow around it instead, set --ag-ui-position: static and place the element in your own grid/flex layout.

docs.title: Page placement
docs.text:
placement="page" turns the widget into a full-screen chat page: a full-bleed background with the conversation in a centred reading column (default ~820px, set via --ag-ui-content-max-width). The assistant turn spans the column width while the user message stays a right-aligned pill. Unlike full (edge-to-edge, left-aligned), it's the layout you want for a dedicated /chat route. Pairs naturally with the answer well.

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" placement="page" data-answer-well></ag-ui-chat>

docs.title: The greeting on an empty page
docs.text:
Until the first message is sent, a page shows a greeting with the composer centred beneath it, and the composer moves to the foot of the page once the conversation has something in it. On a phone it starts at the foot, for the reason below.

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" placement="page" user-name="Ada"></ag-ui-chat>
  • The text is Hello, {name}, filled from user-name, or Hello there when there is no name. Both are string-table keys, greeting and greetingNoName, so strings and data-strings translate them like everything else. user-name is live: a name that arrives after an auth handshake replaces the greeting on screen.
  • Your own greeting goes in slot="greeting", which replaces the text and nothing else. A brand mark belongs there too. The empty slot and data-starters still render beneath it.
  • Styling: the greeting part, plus --ag-ui-greeting-font (default: the widget's font) and --ag-ui-greeting-size (default clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 2.25rem), scaling with the viewport rather than stepping at a breakpoint).
  • data-empty is present on the element while the conversation is empty, for chrome of your own that should react to the same state.
  • Which placements: on by default for page, which is a route of its own. data-greeting="off" restores the plain layout there. embedded opts in with data-greeting (any value but off), for an app shell that gives the panel a page-sized box. The corner placements and the sidebar never show it: a panel opened from a launcher is already mid-task.
  • On a phone the composer stays at the foot, the starters (or your own empty content) sit against it, and the greeting takes the middle of what they leave — the middle of the transcript when there are none. Centring is a shape for a screen with room to spare; at 600px wide and below the room is what the on-screen keyboard takes, and a composer centred over an empty band sits halfway up what is left of the screen, with the prompts that start a conversation nowhere near the field that sends one. data-small-viewport="off" keeps the centred shape at every width, as it keeps the rest of the desktop layout.

The composer's rows stay centred while you type, while a draft grows and while attachments are added, because the centring is two equal flexible halves either side of them and growth splits into both. Nothing in the DOM moves, so focus, the caret and IME composition are unaffected.

Sending is what moves it, not typing, and the composer slides to the foot of the page over --ag-ui-motion (a single frame under reduced motion). Everything else that changes the conversation snaps: a restored conversation mounts docked, picking a thread from the list or continuing a run docks at once, and a new chat returns to the centre at once. While a slow conversation store is still fetching, the page stays docked with the greeting hidden, so a restored conversation never paints the empty layout first.

docs.title: The answer well
docs.text:
Each assistant turn renders inside one .answer group (part answer) that holds its streamed text, tool cards, and pending indicator — so a turn that calls tools reads as a single answer rather than a string of loose siblings. Add the boolean data-answer-well attribute to box that group in a bordered, padded "well"; without it the layout is the flat stack as before. The well is pure CSS and turn-scoped — no JS API — and themeable via --ag-ui-well-bg, --ag-ui-well-border and --ag-ui-well-radius (and ::part(answer)).

The well's corners default to --ag-ui-radius, 12px unless you set it, in every placement. The panel's own frame is different: page and sidebar draw it square because it meets the edge of the window, but nothing inside the panel does, so the well stays round there too. Set --ag-ui-well-radius to round the well differently from the rest of the panel.

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-answer-well></ag-ui-chat>

docs.title: Model reasoning (thoughts)
docs.text:
When a reasoning model streams its chain-of-thought (django-ag-ui forwards it as AG-UI reasoning events — enable a thinking budget via MODEL_SETTINGS, see its docs), the element renders a muted, collapsible thoughts region (part thoughts) at the top of the current answer group. It opens while the model reasons and folds away on the answer's first token; the reader can reopen it. The web component handles the REASONING_* event family (and the retired THINKING_*, which @ag-ui/client still converts onto it, with a console warning, during its deprecation window), so no client config is needed — the thoughts appear whenever the server forwards reasoning.

The header is a toggle only once reasoning has text: a provider that opens and closes reasoning without sending any (redacted thinking, or summaries off) gets a plain label with no body, and no thoughts-toggle part. When reasoning ends the header settles to how long it took, string thoughtFor ("Thought for {seconds}s", the sum of the turn's reasoning rounds); under a second it reads thoughts. A tool call likewise offers its details only over something: with no arguments and a blank result its toggle, and a one-step group's row, are not offered until a result with text arrives.

docs.title: The composer
docs.text:
The composer is one bordered surface (part composer-surface) that owns the border and the focus ring: the field sits on top and grows with what is typed until it hits its ceiling and scrolls, and a tool row (part composer-tools) sits underneath with the paperclip and mic as quiet icon buttons on the left and a circular Send on the right. Send is icon-only — its accessible name still comes from the send / stop strings — and it becomes the Stop control mid-run by swapping its glyph, so nothing moves when a run starts.

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-composer-radius: 14px;
  --ag-ui-composer-max-height: 40vh;  /* where the growing field starts scrolling */
  --ag-ui-tool-btn-size: 30px;        /* the paperclip / mic hit targets */
  --ag-ui-send-size: 30px;            /* the send circle */
  --ag-ui-glyph-size: 18px;
  --ag-ui-glyph-stroke: 1.75;
}

Every glyph is a slot with the built-in mark as its fallback (icon-send, icon-stop, icon-attach, icon-voice), so projecting your own icon set never means restyling a character.

docs.title: Motion
docs.text:
One duration and two curves drive every collapse, expand and slide-over, so the whole widget settles as one thing:

ag-ui-chat {
  --ag-ui-motion: 0.28s;
  --ag-ui-ease: cubic-bezier(0.32, 0.72, 0, 1);      /* the settle */
  --ag-ui-ease-pop: cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.36, 0.64, 1); /* the arrival, with overshoot */
}

Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce the duration collapses to a single frame: states still change, nothing travels. Set --ag-ui-motion: 0s to switch the animation off outright.

docs.title: Voice input
docs.text:
Set data-transcribe-url (django-ag-ui's TranscribeView) to reveal a mic button in the composer (part voice-button). Click it to record via MediaRecorder, click again to stop — the clip is POSTed to the endpoint and the returned transcript is dropped into the textarea. Swap the transport with a custom transcribeHandler — (audio: Blob) => Promise<string> — to use a different STT endpoint or a browser Web Speech adapter without touching the button; when set, the mic appears even with no data-transcribe-url.

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-transcribe-url="/agent/transcribe/"></ag-ui-chat>

docs.title: Theme toggle
docs.text:
theme is a plain attribute you can set yourself, and a host can always drop its own switch into slot="header-actions". For convenience, the boolean data-theme-toggle attribute adds a built-in light⇄dark toggle to the header (part theme-toggle) that flips the scheme word of theme and persists the choice per tab. Only the scheme changes: soft becomes soft dark, soft dark becomes soft light, and auto becomes the opposite of what the system shows, an explicit choice. With no scheme word the toggle flips the scheme the panel is drawn in, so a host rule that sets the element's color-scheme (to follow the page's own dark mode) is flipped from, and the written word then holds against that rule. The toggle's glyph follows a theme the host writes later too, so a host's own picker and the toggle never disagree, and under auto it follows the system's prefers-color-scheme as it changes. One change it cannot see: a host rule that changes the element's color-scheme at runtime (a class swapped on your page, say) fires no event, so the glyph keeps the scheme it last drew until the next click or theme write. Write the scheme word into theme instead, or set theme again after your rule changes. Only the scheme is saved, too: on the next load it is put beside whatever theme name the markup carries, so dark chosen on a soft page restores as classic dark on a classic one. Off by default so it never competes with a host-supplied control.

<ag-ui-chat endpoint="/agent/" data-theme-toggle></ag-ui-chat>

docs.title: The threads contract
docs.text:
data-threads-url points the chat at a server that keeps conversations. This page is the contract that server answers: what RemoteConversationStore (the store the attribute builds) asks for, and what it reads from the answers. It is written from the reference producer, django-ag-ui's ThreadsView (0.89.0), and split into what the component requires and what django-ag-ui adds. Any server that keeps to the first part works.

Every example below is quoted from tests/fixtures/thread_status.json, recorded by scripts/record_thread_status_fixture.py against django-ag-ui 0.89.0 installed from PyPI, with timestamps, ids and ETags replaced by stable stand-ins (etag-1, id-2, times in order).

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
<url> is the attribute's value, ending in a slash (/agent/threads/); <id> is the thread id, URL-encoded. Every request carries the host's headers and credentials.

Route Answers Required by the component GET <url> 200 {"threads": [row, ...]} yes: the conversation list GET <url><id>/ 200 {"thread_id", "messages": [...]}; 404 {"error": "not found"} yes: opening a thread PATCH <url><id>/ with {"title"} 200 {"thread_id", "title"}; 400 on an empty title; 404 rename DELETE <url><id>/ 204; django-ag-ui answers 409 when cancelling a child session fails delete POST <url><id>/read/ 204, or 404 only beside a run store (see thread status) GET <url><id>/children/ 200 {"children": [...]}, 404 django-ag-ui only

An auth refusal is the server's own 401 or 403; django-ag-ui routes it through the same auth seam as the agent endpoint. ?limit= on the list is clamped by django-ag-ui to its configured cap, so a client cannot ask for more than the server allows.

docs.title: The list
docs.text: GET <url> answers 200 with {"threads": [...]}, newest first as the server orders them.

docs.title: Row keys every server sends
docs.text: Key Type Meaning thread_id string The id the detail and mutation routes take. title string Shown in the list. updated_at ISO 8601 string or null Sorts and dates the row. preview string A line of the latest message with text, from any role.

docs.title: Thread status keys
docs.text:
Only beside a run store. A row carries status (idle, running, waiting or failed) and last_read_at (ISO 8601, or null for a thread never read, which the component shows unread unless it is running); reason (string or null) only when failed; interrupts only when waiting, each an AG-UI Interrupt in camelCase.

A waiting approval, as recorded:

{
  "thread_id": "t-approve",
  "title": "Please delete invoice 7",
  "updated_at": "2026-01-01T00:00:04.000000+00:00",
  "preview": "Please delete invoice 7",
  "parent": null,
  "routine": null,
  "agent_id": "helper",
  "status": "waiting",
  "last_read_at": null,
  "interrupts": [
    {
      "id": "int-call-1",
      "reason": "tool_call",
      "message": "delete_invoice",
      "toolCallId": "call-1",
      "metadata": {
        "destructive": true,
        "kind": "approval"
      }
    }
  ],
  "run_id": "r3"
}

A failed row, and an idle one that has been read:

{
  "thread_id": "t-failed",
  "title": "Please fail",
  "updated_at": "2026-01-01T00:00:06.000000+00:00",
  "preview": "Please fail",
  "parent": null,
  "routine": null,
  "agent_id": "helper",
  "status": "failed",
  "last_read_at": null,
  "reason": "error"
}

{
  "thread_id": "t-read",
  "title": "Hello",
  "updated_at": "2026-01-01T00:00:02.000000+00:00",
  "preview": "partial answer and the rest",
  "parent": null,
  "routine": null,
  "agent_id": "helper",
  "status": "idle",
  "last_read_at": "2026-01-01T00:00:01.000000+00:00"
}

An interrupt has id (int-<toolCallId>), reason (tool_call), message, toolCallId and metadata of {"destructive": bool, "kind": "approval" | "question" | "external"}. django-ag-ui writes the approval prompt (or the tool name) as message. A server that keeps the raw call in message may add the prompt as metadata["x-confirm"]: the inbox words an approval row by it.

A listing whose rows carry no status means the server has no run store. The component then sends no read/ POST and never asks for interrupts.

docs.title: What django-ag-ui adds
docs.text:
Optional. The component works without each, and each is read by one feature:

Key Where Read by run_id a waiting row, only when the mount can resume runs (a step store) the inbox's in-place answer, which resumes that run agent_id every row of a mount with an id, beside a run store the agents provider's inbox, to say which agent owns a row parent {"thread_id", "scope"} for a child session, else null (always sent) child sessions listed under their parent thread routine {"id", "name"} for a thread a routine fired, else null (always sent) the routine's name on the row top-level agent {"id", "name", "description"}, beside threads nothing: it names the mount that answered, and the component takes agents from its own directory route GET <url><id>/children/ rows of thread_id, agent_id and status keys not read by the component

The mount's identity object, as recorded:

{
  "id": "helper",
  "name": "Helper",
  "description": "Answers questions."
}

docs.title: Caching: ETag and 304
docs.text:
The list is the polled and streamed resource, so it is conditional.

  • The server sends a strong ETag over the body, Cache-Control: private, no-cache and Vary: Accept.
  • If-None-Match carrying that ETag, *, or the ETag weakened (W/) answers 304 with the ETag and no body.
  • The component keeps its last listing with its ETag. A 304 reuses that listing. A 200 without an ETag header is kept as no listing: the next list is a full GET, and waitingInterrupts asks the server every time.

The recorded 304:

{
  "status": 304,
  "etag": "\"etag-1\"",
  "body": null
}

docs.title: The stream
docs.text:
A list request with Accept: text/event-stream is the live form (data-thread-status="stream").

  • Under ASGI the server answers frames of id: <etag>, then data: <the list body>, then a blank line; Last-Event-ID naming the current ETag skips the unchanged first frame, so a reconnect sends nothing until the list changes. It sends a comment heartbeat when configured and ends after five minutes so the client reconnects and authenticates again.
  • Under WSGI the same request answers plain JSON. The component sees application/json and polls instead.

One recorded frame (the body is abbreviated here; the fixture holds the whole frame):

id: "etag-2"
data: {"threads":[...],"agent":{...}}

The same request with that frame's ETag as Last-Event-ID sent no first frame within the recorder's wait (streamSkipped is null). Under WSGI the answer was 200 with content type application/json.

docs.title: The detail
docs.text:
GET <url><id>/ answers 200 with {"thread_id", "messages": [...]}, the AG-UI messages in camelCase, in order. A missing thread, and another user's thread, are the same answer:

{
  "status": 404,
  "etag": null,
  "body": {
    "error": "not found"
  }
}

The component falls back to its local cache on any non-OK answer, and never asks for a thread it minted and has not sent, so a first visit does not cost a 404.

A thread whose last run finished, as recorded:

{
  "thread_id": "t-approve",
  "messages": [
    {
      "id": "u-r3",
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Please delete invoice 7"
    },
    {
      "id": "id-2",
      "role": "assistant",
      "toolCalls": [
        {
          "id": "call-1",
          "type": "function",
          "function": {
            "name": "delete_invoice",
            "arguments": "{\"target\":\"invoice-7\"}"
          }
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "id": "id-3",
      "role": "tool",
      "content": "deleted invoice-7",
      "toolCallId": "call-1"
    },
    {
      "id": "id-4",
      "role": "assistant",
      "content": "Deleted."
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Restoring a waiting approval
docs.text:
The component offers the approval card for a waiting thread only when every interrupt of the row has a toolCallId and metadata.kind equal to "approval": a resume answers every interrupt, and only approvals can be answered there. A row with one question among them offers none.

The detail must hold the assistant message with that toolCalls entry and no tool message answering it. The recorded messages of the thread parked on call-1:

[
  {
    "id": "u-r3",
    "role": "user",
    "content": "Please delete invoice 7"
  },
  {
    "id": "id-2",
    "role": "assistant",
    "toolCalls": [
      {
        "id": "call-1",
        "type": "function",
        "function": {
          "name": "delete_invoice",
          "arguments": "{\"target\":\"invoice-7\"}"
        }
      }
    ]

]

docs.title: Restoring a pushed chart
docs.text:
messages may carry activity entries, {"id", "role": "activity", "activityType", "content"}, and the component redraws each one it knows (a chart with enableCharts). django-ag-ui does not store pushed activities in the model history on purpose; it materialises them at their anchor when the server is given a thread_activity_source (AGUIServer(thread_activity_source=...), the ThreadActivitySource protocol in django-ag-ui's persistence types). A chart anchored after the user message, as recorded:

{
  "thread_id": "t-chart",
  "messages": [
    {
      "id": "u-r7",
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Chart it"
    },
    {
      "id": "chart-1",
      "role": "activity",
      "activityType": "chart",
      "content": {
        "kind": "bar",
        "series": [
          {
            "name": "Sales",
            "points": [
              1,
              2,
              3
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    },
    {
      "id": "id-5",
      "role": "assistant",
      "content": "partial answer and the rest"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Rename and delete
docs.text:
PATCH <url><id>/ with a JSON {"title": "..."}:

{
  "status": 200,
  "etag": null,
  "body": {
    "thread_id": "t-chart",
    "title": "Sales"
  }
}

An empty or blank title is 400, a missing thread 404:

{
  "status": 400,
  "etag": null,
  "body": {
    "error": "a non-empty 'title' is required"

}

docs.title: Reading a thread
docs.text:
POST <url><id>/read/ marks the thread read and answers 204; an unknown thread answers 404:

{
  "status": 404,

  "body": {
    "error": "not found"
